oneLiner.en: At a pidyon haben, the Rav explains with a Chasam Sofer on Haman that the holiness of Israel is 'reishis', a holiness of the body that cannot be exchanged, and that the pidyon haben reveals this and arouses the redemption of Hashem's firstborn.

abstract.en: The Rav repeats a Chasam Sofer on Haman's words 'there is one people scattered among the nations': Haman thought Israel's holiness was a holiness of value, which can be redeemed or exchanged, and that scattered among seventy nations it would be nullified. But Israel is 'reishis', with a holiness of the body. This holiness of reishis is the whole matter of the Exodus, when Israel was called Hashem's firstborn and the mitzvah of sanctifying and redeeming the firstborn was given. Hashem may place Israel's suffering on the nations, but Israel itself cannot be exchanged, as Bilaam wished. The Rav explains Rashi's sharpness against one who says terumah can be redeemed. He then says the firstborn is the reishis from which the blessing of the later children flows, and that the pidyon haben arouses Hashem's redemption of Israel, and closes with a prayer for the final redemption.

en: Following the Chasam Sofer, Haman thought Israel had only a holiness of value, which can be exchanged or nullified among the nations.
Israel is 'reishis', with a holiness of the body that cannot be exchanged, and this is the whole matter of the Exodus.
Hashem can transfer what is decreed on Israel onto the nations, but Israel itself cannot be exchanged for another nation.
The firstborn is the reishis from which the blessing of the later children comes, and the pidyon haben reveals Israel's holiness of reishis and arouses the redemption.

title.en: Haman and the holiness of reishis

summary.en: The Rav repeats the Chasam Sofer that Haman thought Israel's holiness could be exchanged or nullified among seventy nations, but Israel is 'reishis', with a holiness of the body. This holiness is the matter of the Exodus and of the firstborn, and while Israel's suffering can be transferred to the nations, Israel itself cannot be exchanged, as Bilaam wished.

title.en: Redeeming terumah, the firstborn and the redemption

summary.en: The Rav asks why Rashi is so sharp against one who says terumah can be redeemed, and answers that Israel is 'reishis', and those who hold that reishis can be redeemed are Bilaam and his students. He explains that the firstborn is the reishis from which later children's blessing comes, and that the pidyon haben arouses Hashem's redemption of Israel, closing with a prayer for the final redemption.

oneLiner.en: At a pidyon haben, the Rav explains that holiness hidden in parents is revealed in their children, and that both havdalah and pidyon haben protect a place from which holiness has departed.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara on how many havdalos one says, where Rabbi Menachem bar Simai, called 'the son of holy ones', says only one. He was called this because he never looked at the image on a coin, and the Yerushalmi says he never did so at all, so he was born that way and drew the holiness from his parents. The Rav explains with the Ramban on 'a root bearing gall and wormwood' that what is hidden in parents comes out openly in the children: his parents never thought about money, so their son would not even look at it. He then brings the Or HaChaim on why tumas ohel applies to Jews: where great holiness departed, the impure forces gather. Every motza'ei Shabbos the extra soul leaves, so people make three havdalos for protection, while Rabbi Menachem needed only one to fulfil the mitzvah. Finally he links pidyon haben to 'pedus' as separation, and blesses the family.

en: Rabbi Menachem bar Simai never looked at the image on a coin, and since he never did so even as a child, his holiness came from his parents.
What is hidden and inward in the parents becomes openly revealed in the children.
A place from which great holiness has departed draws the forces of impurity, which is why tumas ohel applies to Jews.
Havdalah protects the place left empty when the extra soul of Shabbos departs; ordinary people say three havdalos, while Rabbi Menachem needed only one.
Pidyon haben is connected to 'pedus', which the commentators read as a separation, like havdalah, between Jews and the nations.

title.en: The 'son of holy ones' and inherited holiness

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara about Rabbi Menachem bar Simai, who never looked at the image on a coin, and asks why he is called 'son of holy ones'. Using the Ramban on 'a root bearing gall and wormwood', he explains that what is hidden in parents is revealed in their children.

title.en: Havdalah and the empty place left by Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains havdalah as protection against the forces of impurity when the extra soul of Shabbos departs, bringing the Or HaChaim on tumas ohel. Ordinary people make three havdalos, but Rabbi Menachem bar Simai needed only one, to fulfil the mitzvah.

title.en: Pidyon haben as a separation, and a brachah

summary.en: The Rav connects 'pedus' in the passuk to a separation between Jews and the nations, and explains that the firstborn must be redeemed because the holiness meant for him has departed. He closes by blessing the child that the holiness of his parents be revealed in him.

catalogTitle: ”כי קרוב אליך הדבר וכו'” למה כל כך קשה לקיים תורה ומצות? והתירוץ - “עצבות.” עצות להיות בשמחה. כל יסורים באים מב' אותיות ראשונות שבשם הוי'.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, on the end of Tanya chapter 25, how a Jew's readiness to give his life rather than worship idols makes every mitzvah 'very near', and why both the aveirah and the union of a mitzvah are eternal, while teshuvah restores the bond.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews that all positive mitzvos branch out of 'Anochi Hashem' and all prohibitions out of 'Lo yihyeh lecha', so every aveirah cuts a Jew off from Hashem as idolatry would. Since every Jew is ready to give his life against avodah zarah, he can tell himself, facing a temptation, that the far smaller sacrifice of giving up a desire is surely within reach; this is how 'ki karov eilecha hadavar' is fulfilled. Even a 'temporary' aveirah is not temporary, since above time everything is eternal. He explains bittul and 'Hashem Echad', the world as a mirage of hester panim, and that the union of a mitzvah, like the Torah, is eternal, while teshuvah undoes the cutting off. He admits the idea is hard for minds molded by this world. He then discusses why Selach Lanu is said three times a day, why the Tanya speaks of positive mitzvos, achta v'ashuv, why Moshe taught 'b'chol nafshecha' before Eretz Yisrael, and answers a question on teshuvah and forgiveness.

en: All positive mitzvos are branches of 'Anochi Hashem' and all prohibitions of 'Lo yihyeh lecha', so any aveirah detaches a Jew from Hashem as idolatry does.

Since a Jew is ready to give his life rather than worship idols, he can reason that giving up a smaller desire, a lesser 'mesiras nefesh', is surely within his power; this makes serving Hashem 'very near'.
Above, Hashem and His will are beyond time, so an aveirah 'just for now' is registered forever, and so is the union of a mitzvah and the Torah itself.
An aveirah cuts a person off eternally, but teshuvah removes the cutting off and he is again eternally attached.
Selach Lanu is repeated three times a day because there is most likely bittul Torah in between, and because a person who grows needs new forgiveness for what he did before.
Moshe Rabbeinu taught 'b'chol nafshecha' to the Jews entering Eretz Yisrael so they could use the reckoning of mesiras nefesh against every other temptation there.

title.en: Mesiras nefesh makes every mitzvah near

summary.en: The Rav reviews that every mitzvah is a branch of the first two commandments, so every aveirah detaches a Jew from Hashem. Since every Jew stands ready to die rather than worship idols, he can tell himself that giving up a smaller desire is surely within reach; this is how 'ki karov eilecha hadavar' is fulfilled.

title.en: No such thing as a temporary aveirah

summary.en: The Rav explains the Tanya's point that a Jew must give his life even for idolatry 'only for now', after which he would do teshuvah. Above, past, present and future are one, so an aveirah, and also refraining from one, is registered as eternal.

title.en: Bittul and Hashem Echad

summary.en: The Rav explains that the purpose of avodas Hashem is to be nullified to Hashem: 'Echad' means there is nothing but Him, and the world that seems to exist on its own is a mirage, hester panim. One who gives up his desires to cleave to Hashem merits gilui panim and feels it in his soul.

title.en: The eternal union and the eternal Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the union formed when a person withstands a desire is eternal, because Hashem and His will, expressed in the Torah, are above time and never change. An aveirah cuts a person off eternally, but teshuvah restores the bond; he answers a listener's question and compares the Torah's changing appearance to a cloud.

title.en: Accepting a hard idea with emunah

summary.en: The Rav admits that this half page is hard to grasp, not because the logic is weak but because minds molded by this world take it as the world of truth. He says one must accept it with emunah, as one moves on past a difficult Tosafos, and warns that the next chapter will be similar.

title.en: Why Selach Lanu three times a day

summary.en: The Rav asks why Selach Lanu is said three times a day if Hashem surely forgives the first time. He answers with the Tanya that even a masmid interrupts his learning in between, so new bittul Torah needs new forgiveness, and a deep teshuvah need not be repeated.

title.en: Growing teshuvah, stains, and achta v'ashuv

summary.en: The Rav adds that one who grows is held to account again for old aveiros, and Yom Kippur brings teshuvah from a higher root. He explains that the Tanya speaks of positive mitzvos because prohibitions leave a stain needing more, with parables of a stained shirt and a broken bottle of wine. A person who knows he will likely fall again is not 'achta v'ashuv'.

title.en: B'chol nafshecha before Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav asks why Moshe Rabbeinu commanded 'b'chol nafshecha' in Krias Shema to Jews about to enter Eretz Yisrael, where they were promised victory and faced no forced idolatry. He answers that it was an eitzah: the reckoning of readiness for mesiras nefesh would help them withstand every other temptation there.

title.en: Teshuvah first, then forgiveness

summary.en: Answering a listener, the Rav explains that teshuvah comes first and the request for forgiveness after it, so the bracha is made knowing it is accepted. He mentions vidui in Tachanun for individual sins and one collective sin, and says that unlike other requests, forgiveness is guaranteed.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the seudah of a pidyon haben, unlike Esav's feast over despising the bechorah, honors the Jewish people's status as Hashem's firstborn, His 'reishis', and that even the last generations share in that status.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the custom of performing the pidyon haben in the middle of the seudah for publicity, and asks why this mitzvah needs more publicity than others. He turns to the parsha of the festivals, where the Torah interrupts the omer and Shavuos with the mitzvos of leket and peah. He then explains that Esav's sin in despising the bechorah was a flaw in his outlook, since the bechorah stands for the chosenness of Israel, the 'reishis' for whose sake the world was created. Esav even made a feast over it; the seudah of pidyon haben does the opposite and shows honor for the bechorah, which is greater than the mitzvah itself. The theme of reishis runs from Pesach to Shavuos. The forgotten sheaves and the corner of the field stand for the last generations, which are as precious as the first fruits, and the seudah is a chizuk in these times.

en: The custom is to perform the pidyon haben in the middle of the seudah, as a matter of publicizing the mitzvah.
The bechorah stands for the chosenness of Israel, called 'reishis', for whose sake the whole world was created.
Esav's despising of the bechorah was a sin of outlook, not of desire or anger, and only an Esav can stumble in it.
The seudah of pidyon haben is the reverse of Esav's feast: Jews make a seudah to honor the bechorah.
Honoring the bechorah is greater than the mitzvah of the bechorah itself, as honor of the Torah is greater than its study.
The last generations, like the forgotten sheaves and the corner of the field, are as precious to Hashem as the first fruits.

title.en: Why the pidyon haben is done mid-seudah

summary.en: The Rav notes that, unlike other mitzvos, the pidyon haben is performed in the middle of the seudah for publicity, and asks why. He turns to the parsha of the festivals, the omer and the count to Shavuos, and to Rashi's question why leket and peah interrupt the festivals.

title.en: Esav despised the bechorah

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah stresses that Esav despised the bechorah while not mentioning the five grave sins he did that day. He explains that the bechorah is the chosenness of Israel, the 'reishis' for which the world was created, and that the bechorah belongs to whoever wants to serve Hashem.

title.en: A sin of outlook, and Esav's feast

summary.en: Through Rav Tzadok's reading of the Chazal on techiyas hameisim, the Rav explains that despising the bechorah is a symptom of having no share in it, a sin only an Esav commits. Esav even made a feast over it, and the seudah of pidyon haben expresses the opposite: a Jew's joy in his share in Israel's 'reishis'.

title.en: Honor of the bechorah, and Esav's false reishis

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Megillah that honor of the Torah outweighs its study, and says the seudah, honoring the bechorah, is greater than the mitzvah itself. He shows that reishis runs through many mitzvos, and that Esav's and Amalek's 'reishis' is false, as shown by its lack of a good end.

title.en: From Pesach to Shavuos: the festival of reishis

summary.en: The Rav describes the time from Pesach to Shavuos as one long festival of reishis, in which a Jew identifies with Hashem's first 'produce' through the omer and the bikkurim. He then turns to the last generations, in a time of great hester panim, when it is hard to see that Jews are Hashem's reishis.

title.en: The last sheaves are also reishis

summary.en: The Rav explains that leket, shikchah and peah, the last grain of the field, stand for the last generations, which are as precious as the first fruits; this answers why they appear among the festivals. He concludes that a seudah of pidyon haben in these last generations is a great chizuk, and closes with a brachah for the true redemption.

oneLiner.en: At a pidyon haben, the Rav explains that 'pedus', redemption, comes after the alphabetical order of the Tehillim is complete, showing that Hashem leads the Jewish people above the natural order, and that a pidyon haben is a segulah for salvation.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by saying that pidyon haben is a matter beyond explanation, and that its parsha comes from yetzias Mitzrayim and is written in the tefillin, shel rosh and shel yad. Bringing the Pri Tzaddik, he explains that creation runs on an order, the order of the aleph-beis. In the chapter of Tehillim 'I will bless Hashem at all times', the verses follow the aleph-beis to its end, and only then comes an added verse, 'Hashem redeems the soul of His servants'; the same happens in the chapter ending 'G-d, redeem Israel from all its troubles'. Redemption is thus a conduct above the order, Hashem's special way with the Jewish people. He adds that in the days of Shabbos Mevarchim Tamuz, times of strict judgment, a pidyon haben is a great segulah for the community and for those at the simcha, and closes with blessings for the family and for the complete redemption.

en: The parsha of pidyon haben comes from yetzias Mitzrayim and is part of the tefillin.
In Tehillim, the verse about redemption is added after the aleph-beis order is complete, showing that redemption is above the order.
Hashem conducts Himself with the Jewish people in a special way that is not bound by the order of creation.
In the days around Shabbos Mevarchim Tamuz, times of strict judgment, a pidyon haben is a great segulah for the community and for those who come to it.

title.en: Redemption beyond the aleph-beis order

summary.en: The Rav says pidyon haben comes from yetzias Mitzrayim and is in the tefillin, then brings the Pri Tzaddik: in two alphabetical chapters of Tehillim, a verse of redemption is added after the aleph-beis ends, showing that redemption is above the order of creation.

title.en: A segulah in days of judgment, and blessings

summary.en: The Rav explains that redemption is Hashem's conduct above the order with the Jewish people, and that a pidyon haben around Shabbos Mevarchim Tamuz, a time of judgment, is a segulah for salvation for the community and for those present. He closes with blessings for the family and for the complete redemption.

oneLiner.en: Using the tradition that the ten sedras of Devarim correspond to the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, the Rav reads the current century in Nitzavim-Vayelech: the hester panim of the Holocaust, the promise that the Torah will not be forgotten, and the geulah that is written before the galus.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that everything Moshe Rabbeinu foretold in Devarim about exile and return has come true, while the nations' scriptures avoid predictions, and the church now has a problem with Jews back in Eretz Yisroel and Jerusalem. He then brings a tradition in the name of the Vilna Gaon that the ten sedras of Devarim correspond to the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, the world's Erev Shabbos, with Nitzavim-Vayelech counted as one sedra and corresponding to the present century. He tells how, as a bochur on Rosh Hashanah of that century's first year, he learned that Hitler had invaded Poland. In Vayelech he reads the double hester panim, explained with a mashal of a child who does not even know his father is hiding, and the promise that the Torah will never be forgotten. Finally he asks why the geulah of Nitzavim precedes the galus of Vayelech, and answers from the Gemara that for Jews the cure comes before the blow. He closes urging the bochurim to prepare for Moshiach.

en: Everything Moshe Rabbeinu foretold about the Jewish people's exile and return has been fulfilled, while the nations' scriptures do not dare to predict the future.
The ten sedras of Devarim correspond to the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, and Nitzavim-Vayelech, counted as one sedra, corresponds to the present century.
The doubled hester panim in Vayelech means that even the hiding itself is hidden, which the Rav calls the confused state of Jews after the Holocaust.
The promise that the Torah will not be forgotten from the mouths of Jewish children has held, while the cultures of the great nations have been forgotten.
For Jews Hashem prepares the cure before the blow, which is why the geulah of Nitzavim is written before the galus of Vayelech.
Moshiach is near, and the Rav says one must prepare for him like for Shabbos: teshuvah, Torah and mitzvos, and good davening.

title.en: Moshe's prophecies fulfilled before our eyes

summary.en: The Rav notes that everything Moshe Rabbeinu foretold in Devarim about exile and return has come true, while the nations' scriptures avoid predictions. He describes the church's problem with Jews, many of them Torah-observant, back in Eretz Yisroel and the Old City of Jerusalem.

title.en: The ten sedras of Devarim and the ten centuries

summary.en: The Rav brings in the name of the Vilna Gaon that the ten sedras of Devarim correspond to the ten centuries of the sixth millennium, the world's Erev Shabbos, with Nitzavim-Vayelech counted as one sedra. He tells of Rav Chaim of Volozhin asking the Gaon where he is hinted in Ki Seitzei, and concludes that the present century is found in Nitzavim-Vayelech.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah when Hitler entered Poland

summary.en: The Rav recounts how, as a bochur at the start of this century, he davened with his father on Rosh Hashanah and saw the congregation weeping because Hitler had invaded Poland. The war expected to last weeks lasted five years, and six million Jews were killed; the start of the century must therefore be found in Nitzavim-Vayelech.

title.en: Hester panim within hester panim

summary.en: The Rav reads the pesukim in Vayelech where Hashem foretells that He will hide His face and many evils will befall the people, and asks what the doubled hiding means. With a mashal of a child chased by a tiger who does not even know his father is inside, he explains it as hiding within hiding, the state of Jews who lost their emunah in the Holocaust.

title.en: The song as witness; the Torah will not be forgotten

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem commands writing the song of Ha'azinu as a witness that He foretold the troubles, and promises the Torah will not be forgotten from the Jews' children. The cultures of Rome, Greece and Bavel are forgotten while Jews still learn Torah, even though Hitler specifically targeted the yeshivos and talmidei chachamim.

title.en: Why the geulah comes before the galus

summary.en: The Rav reads the promise of return and ingathering in Nitzavim and asks two questions: why this century is split over two sedras, and why the geulah in Nitzavim precedes the galus in Vayelech. He answers both from the Gemara that for Jews the cure comes before the blow, illustrated by Esther and Mordechai, a surgeon and a mohel, and explains that galus and geulah are two separate themes.

title.en: Preparing for Moshiach on the world's Erev Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav tells the bochurim that Moshiach is near, comparing the world to a barrel of gunpowder with a lit fuse. Like Erev Shabbos, one must do teshuvah, put on the Shabbos clothes of Torah and mitzvos, and daven well with a minyan, starting together word by word; he urges them to make a kiddush Hashem on their Shabbos away and closes with l'chaim.

catalogTitle: אגרת "להשכילך בינה" - בענין בני חיי מזוני כתוב - “בטל רצונך מפני רצונו.” יש צער אחד שהוא אמת וזה צער שעבר רצון ה'. ומכל מקום - אל תעסוק בו הרבה.

oneLiner.en: The Rav learns Tanya chapter 26: the yetzer hara can only be overpowered with the alertness that comes from simcha, the only true sadness is remorse over aveiros at set times, and worldly suffering is relieved by knowing it comes from the hidden world.

abstract.en: The Rav reviews how chapter 25 made serving Hashem seem easy, then turns to chapter 26: like a wrestler, or an ox against a lion, the lazy side loses, so the yetzer hara can only be overcome with alertness born of simcha, while sadness itself breeds craving. Sadness has an advantage only when it is remorse over aveiros, and only for its product, teshuvah and the joy of reconciliation, felt at set times such as Tikkun Chatzos, which the Rav explains at length. Sadness over livelihood or other worldly matters, by the Tanya's standard, is nothing. The remedy is to know that hardships come from the hidden world, too high for this world to bear, and to accept them with simcha, as the stories of the Ger Tzedek Graf Potocki and of the Alter Rebbe's arrest show. The Rav admits this level is very hard for our generation.

en: Like a wrestler who loses when he is lazy and heavy even if he is stronger, a person can only overpower the yetzer hara with alertness that comes from simcha and an open heart.
Sadness itself feeds the yetzer hara, because an unhappy person seeks gratification elsewhere.
The only true sadness is remorse over aveiros, and its value lies only in what it produces: teshuvah and the simcha that follows it.
Even this remorse belongs only to set times, such as before sleep or Rosh Hashanah, and not all day.
Sadness over children, health or livelihood has no place by the Tanya's standard, since Hashem's hashgachah pratis puts a person where it is best for him.
Hardships come from the hidden world, which is higher than the revealed one; one who accepts them with simcha will see them transformed into revealed kindness.

title.en: Is it a cinch? The wrestler and the lion

summary.en: The Rav reviews chapter 25, that every aveirah separates a person from Hashem like avodah zarah, which seems to make being a tzaddik easy. He then opens chapter 26 with the wrestling analogy: a stronger fighter who is lazy and heavy loses, as an ox loses to a lion.

title.en: Overpowering the yetzer hara with simcha

summary.en: The Rav explains that laziness comes from sadness and a stone-like heart, while alertness comes from simcha in knowing one has a Provider in heaven. He shows how sadness itself drives a person to seek gratification, and says the Tanya's demand for a heart free of worry applies, to our degree, even in our generation.

title.en: The one true sadness: remorse over aveiros

summary.en: The Rav explains the passuk that every sorrow has an advantage: not that sadness is good, but that remorse over aveiros leads to teshuvah and the simcha of reconciliation, like two friends who make up. This sadness belongs only at set times, and he reads it into the pesukim of Tehillim 51 about a broken spirit leading to joy.

title.en: Tikkun Chatzos and the seudah of Dovid HaMelech

summary.en: The Rav explains Tikkun Chatzos, Dovid HaMelech's midnight tefillah, and parallels the tefillos of the Avos and of Dovid to the Shabbos seudos and Melaveh Malkah. Tehillim 51 is part of Tikkun Chatzos, where a person laments the churban and, more deeply, his own inner Beis HaMikdash ruined by his aveiros, and then rises to simcha.

title.en: Light after darkness; worldly sadness is nothing

summary.en: The Rav explains that joy after sadness is like light after darkness, and brings the curse for not serving Hashem with simcha. By the Tanya's standard, sadness over income or other worldly matters is a child's complaint over a broken house of blocks; he asks whether a person is sad over his aveiros or over his income, and admits this chapter demands more than we can offer.

title.en: Bnei, chayei, mezonei and the hidden world

summary.en: The Rav asks how a person can free himself from sadness over children, life and sustenance, and brings Chazal that one must bless and accept the bad with simcha as the good. He explains the two halves of the Shem Havayah, the hidden world and the revealed world: hardships come from the higher, hidden world, which this world cannot bear, and they bring a person closer to Hashem.

title.en: Those who rejoice in suffering

summary.en: The Rav explains that accepting hardship with simcha turns the hidden into revealed kindness, and that a person should say even of undesirable things that they are for the good. He brings the Gemara about those who accept suffering with love, and the passuk that those who love Hashem are like the sun going out in its strength: the tzaddik feels the pressure like a tight shoe but disregards it in his joy of closeness to Hashem.

title.en: The Ger Tzedek and the house of blocks

summary.en: The Rav tells briefly of Graf Potocki, a great Polish lord who became a Jew and was condemned to be burned. When the executioner asked whether he would take revenge, he answered with a parable of children's houses of blocks: this world is worth nothing to him, and he is going to a better world.

title.en: The sun drawn from its sheath

summary.en: The Rav explains that for such tzaddikim all suffering is suffering of love, and that the spiritual sun will be uncovered from its sheath, so the hidden world will shine in this world on those who take refuge in Hashem's shadow. He sums up the Tanya's remedy: realize that worldly hardships are nothing and be happy with Hashem who is hidden in them.

title.en: Reb Shmuel Munkes and the Alter Rebbe's arrest

summary.en: The Rav admits this level is not for everybody, then tells how Reb Shmuel Munkes told the Alter Rebbe not to hide from arrest: if he is a Rebbe he need fear nothing, and if not, by what right did he take away thousands of Jews' appreciation of this world. He concludes that this paragraph may not be for our generation, and that other aids to simcha must be found.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to bachurim before Rosh Hashana, the Rav explains that each Rosh Hashana the world is created anew and judged by its place in Hashem's kingship, that the heart of the day is accepting His kingship as in Shema Yisroel, and that Elul is the preparation for it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by warning that the coming Rosh Hashana is a fateful one: seventy years earlier the war began and six million Jews perished, and the concealment of what was coming was part of the decree. Now Iran openly threatens Eretz Yisroel, and although a Midrash and a pasuk promise that no weapon against Israel will succeed, a promise still needs tefilah, as Eliyahu davened at the altar despite Hashem's promise. Every Rosh Hashana judges everything, even a shtender. He urges the bachurim to thank Hashem for their portion in yeshiva, to daven for all Jews, and to make the last two Shabbosos holy. He then explains that each Rosh Hashana the world is created anew, and each thing is judged by whether it belongs to Hashem's kingship. Rosh Hashana's mitzvah is kabbalas ol malchus shamayim, expressed in Shema Yisroel, the tenth pasuk of Malchuyos. Elul is the preparation, as one prepares for Shema in Shacharis, and real learning depends on good davening.

en: Even when there is a promise of protection, as for Klal Yisroel now, tefilah is needed for the promise to take effect, as Eliyahu davened despite Hashem's promise.
Each Rosh Hashana the world is created anew for one year, just as Adam was created on the first Rosh Hashana.
On Rosh Hashana every part of creation is judged by whether it belongs to Hashem's kingship, and a Jew is judged by how far he accepts Hashem as his King.
The mitzvah of Rosh Hashana is kabbalas ol malchus shamayim, accepting the yoke of Heaven's kingship, whose essence is Shema Yisroel.
Rosh Hashana is the Shema of the whole year, and Elul is the preparation for it, as the long morning prayers prepare for Shema.
Learning becomes true learning only after good davening; without it, learning can be driven by honor and competition.

candidateTopics: renewal of creation on Rosh Hashana

title.en: A fateful Rosh Hashana and the threat of Iran

summary.en: The Rav says the coming Rosh Hashana is fateful, recalls that the war began seventy years earlier and that not knowing what was coming was part of the decree, and describes Iran's open threat against Eretz Yisroel. He brings a Midrash and the pasuk that no weapon formed against Israel will succeed.

title.en: A promise still needs tefilah

summary.en: The Rav says that even with a promise one must daven, proving it from Eliyahu, who davened for the miracle at his altar although Hashem had promised it. Every Rosh Hashana judges everything, as Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin said even his shtender is judged, and in these times of ikvesa d'meshicha a great judgment awaits Klal Yisroel.

title.en: Gratitude, responsibility and two holy Shabbosos

summary.en: The Rav tells the bachurim to thank Hashem daily that they sit in the beis medrash, with parents who sacrifice so they can learn, and says this gives them the responsibility to daven for a good year for all Jews. He urges them to make the two remaining Shabbosos before Rosh Hashana holy by preparing for them through the week.

title.en: The world is created anew each Rosh Hashana

summary.en: From 'this day is the beginning of Your works', the Rav explains that each Rosh Hashana repeats the first one, when Adam was created and the world's fate depended on him. At the end of the year nothing sustains the world, the night of Rosh Hashana is a time of fearsome judgment, and with the tefillos and shofar the world is created anew and Hashem is crowned King.

title.en: Judged by one's place in Hashem's kingship

summary.en: The Rav explains that a thing exists only as part of Hashem's kingship, so a Jew who accepts to obey Hashem in learning, davening and guarding himself is inscribed for a good year, while one who does not has no real existence. Even inanimate things have a life-force from Hashem and are judged, which is why something may break after Rosh Hashana.

title.en: Each day's mitzvah, and Rosh Hashana's

summary.en: The Rav brings that each day of the year has its own mitzvah, corresponding to the 365 negative mitzvos; from the Zohar, Tisha B'Av corresponds to gid hanasheh, Esav's portion, and Jews do not eat it. He proposes that Rosh Hashana's mitzvah is kerias Shema, since it is the day of kabbalas ol malchus shamayim, and the first of the ten days of creation includes them all.

title.en: Shema, the tenth pasuk of Malchuyos

summary.en: The Rav describes the ten pesukim of Malchuyos, Zichronos and Shofaros and the sweet, long Musaf, and asks why the tenth pasuk of Malchuyos, Shema Yisroel, lacks the word melech. As the Gemara counts Bereishis as a maamar without 'vayomer', Shema is the root acceptance through which Hashem becomes King; it is emunah, like Anochi, and Rosh Hashana is the Shema of the year.

title.en: Elul as preparation; davening before learning

summary.en: The Rav explains that the night Shema only renews what the morning Shema accomplished, and that the long morning prayers prepare for Shema, as Elul prepares for Rosh Hashana. He urges the bachurim to prepare with extra davening, says that without good davening learning is not true learning, and closes with a blessing for a good year.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to bachurim, the Rav teaches that a Jew is measured by his bein adam lachaveiro, and that guarding the honor of another Jew, as Rachel and Tamar did, is what brings salvation to Klal Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by praising the bachurim's achdus at a Shabbos tisch, which impressed a guest from Miami, and notes the awe of Shabbos. He then warns that the generation is weak in bein adam lachaveiro: machlokes, rechilus and the Jewish magazines. An honest Jew is measured by how he treats others, since Rabbi Akiva calls 'love your fellow as yourself' the great rule of the Torah, and the Torah was given when Israel was one. One must love even a sinner, hating only his deeds, as the Chasam Sofer wrote of his own battles. A group can say 'the world was created for us' and bring Moshiach. He brings Rabbi Eliezer's dying charge to honor one's friends, and Beis Hillel, who merited the halachah for mentioning Beis Shammai first. The center is the Midrash of Rachel, whose giving the signs to Leah saved the Jews when the Avos could not. He adds Moshe's 'choose for us', Shaul's 'for us', honoring every creature, and Tamar, who would rather be burned than shame Yehudah.

en: The Rav says an honest Jew is measured by his bein adam lachaveiro, since Rabbi Akiva calls 'love your fellow as yourself' the great rule of the Torah.
One must love every Jew, even a sinner: hate the bad deed, not the person.
Rabbi Eliezer's final charge to his students was to guard the honor of their friends, more than learning, davening or tzedakah.
Rachel's giving the signs to Leah, so that her sister would not be shamed, brought about the promise that the Jews will return from exile when the merit of the Avos did not.
Every creature must be respected because Hashem made it with great wisdom, and certainly every Jew.
Tamar's readiness to be burned rather than shame Yehudah teaches that one may never embarrass another Jew.

title.en: Pride in the bachurim's achdus

summary.en: The Rav recalls that the beis medrash gives bachurim the best seats to strengthen their tefillah, and says he wants to speak this time about bein adam lachaveiro. He tells how a guest from Miami was amazed at the bachurim sitting together in achdus at the Shabbos Bereishis tisch, and connects their awe to the Yerushalmi on the fear of Shabbos.

title.en: A Jew is measured by bein adam lachaveiro

summary.en: The Rav laments the generation's weakness in bein adam lachaveiro: machlokes, rechilus and the magazines read on Shabbos. He says a person is not measured by his special chickens but by how he treats others, bringing Rabbi Akiva's 'love your fellow as yourself is a great rule of the Torah' and 'Ata echad'.

title.en: Love every Jew; a chevra can bring Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah was given when Israel camped 'as one man with one heart', that machlokes is a great kelipah, and that one must love even a sinner while hating his deeds, citing the Kotzker, 'love covers all sins', Tanna Devei Eliyahu and the Chasam Sofer. He says the yetzer hara for machlokes is strong in this generation, and that a chevra should say 'the world was created for us' and strive to bring Moshiach.

title.en: Rabbi Eliezer's charge and Beis Hillel

summary.en: The Rav tells how the dying Rabbi Eliezer told his students to be careful with the honor of their friends, more than with learning, davening or tzedakah. He then brings the Gemara that the halachah follows Beis Hillel because they were gentle and mentioned Beis Shammai's words before their own.

title.en: Rachel's tears and the signs she gave Leah

summary.en: From the haftarah 'a voice is heard in Ramah', the Rav tells the Midrash: when the Jews served idols, Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov pleaded in vain, until Rachel told Hashem she gave her signs to Leah so her sister would not be shamed, and Hashem promised the children would return. He stresses that this act did what the Avos' great nisyonos did not, and says one should stop and cry over it.

title.en: Treating others as equals; honoring every creature

summary.en: The Rav shows that Moshe told Yehoshua 'choose for us', treating his student as an equal, and that Shaul merited kingship for saying his father would worry 'for us', including his servant. He brings Tanna Devei Eliyahu that no creature may be disgraced, describes the wisdom in a rat, gives the Midrash's mashal of an artist whose painting is mocked, and concludes that every Jew, made with such wisdom, must be honored.

title.en: Tamar, and the closing call to achdus

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara learned from Tamar, who did not name Yehudah even as she was taken to be burned, that it is better to be thrown into a furnace than to shame another in public. He asks how anyone can then mock or hurt another Jew, and closes with 'Ata echad' said at Shabbos Minchah and Rabbi Akiva's great rule.

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that Hashem would not listen to Bilaam's claims against the Jewish people because 'Hashem your G-d loves you', and that Shabbos Balak is a Shabbos to feel that love, which covers all sins.

abstract.en: The Rav notes that Parshas Balak usually falls in days opposite to simcha, and is a comfort: Hashem turned the curse into a blessing. This year the arrangement is unusual, and by hashgachah pratis Jews now need this parsha, since every individual needs salvation: healing, shidduchim, children and more. These hardships come from accusations against a Jew, yet Hashem can turn them to blessing. The navi adds 'My people, remember what Balak counselled', and Bilaam came with claims, perhaps justified, but Hashem would not listen, because He loves us, as a father will not hear claims against his child; love covers all sins. The Rav asks that this Shabbos a Jew not feel distant from Hashem in his troubles, and go toward Him with love. He ends with the Rambam that no sin offering is brought on Shabbos, because Shabbos is a day of love.

en: Parshas Balak is a comfort, because Hashem turned the curse into a blessing.
The hardships of individuals come from accusations against a Jew, but Hashem can turn even these into blessing.
Hashem would not listen to Bilaam's claims, perhaps justified, because He loves the Jewish people as a father loves his child.
'Love covers all sins': there are sins, but the love covers them.
Shabbos is a day of love, and therefore, as the Rav brings from the Rambam, no sin offering is brought on it.

summary.en: The Rav notes that Parshas Balak usually falls in days opposite to simcha and comforts with the curse turned to blessing. This year's unusual arrangement is hashgachah pratis: every Jew needs salvation, and Hashem can turn the accusations behind hardships into blessing.

title.en: 'Remember what Balak counselled': love covers sins

summary.en: The Rav brings the navi's plea 'My people, remember what Balak counselled', and explains that Hashem refused to hear Bilaam's perhaps justified claims because He loves us, as a father will not hear claims against his child; love covers all sins.

title.en: A Shabbos of love

summary.en: The Rav asks that this Shabbos a Jew reflect on Hashem's unearned love and not feel cut off from Him in his troubles, but go toward Him with love. He brings the Rambam that no sin offering is brought on Shabbos because it is a day of love, and closes with a blessing for the Shabbos.

catalogTitle: Shabbos - A Day That Sings For Itself (Intro.to the תפילות of שבת)

oneLiner.en: Introducing the tefillos of Shabbos, the Rav explains that tefillah is the service of the heart that connects us to the Avos, and that Shabbos, the seventh, is the day that sings for itself.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the mitzvah to serve Hashem with the heart, which Chazal call tefillah. The Avos instituted the three tefillos, the karbanos correspond to them, and the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah composed the nusach; the first bracha connects us to the Avos. He brings the machlokes of the Rambam and the Ramban on the daily mitzvah of tefillah, and stresses that tefillah requires kavanah, knowing the words and putting one's heart into them. Tefillah has endless depths, and the Arizal writes that each tefillah until Moshiach is different. He discusses davening without kavanah, especially in the first bracha. Learning Sefer Bereishis likewise connects us to the Avos. Shabbos, the day of avodas Hashem, drops the twelve weekday brachos that parallel the shevatim and reaches back to the Avos. Kabbalas Shabbos culminates in Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbos: Shabbos sings for itself, as the seventh note completes the harp of creation.

en: Tefillah is the avodah of the heart; a tefillah said without the heart, the Rav says, is not called tefillah.
The first bracha of Shemoneh Esrei connects us to the Avos, who instituted tefillah, and this is the introduction to all of tefillah.
The nusach of tefillah was composed by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah with ruach hakodesh, and its depths are endless, like pshat, drush and remez in Torah.
On Shabbos the twelve middle brachos, which parallel the twelve shevatim and deal with bodily needs, are replaced by one bracha asking only for spiritual closeness, going back to the Avos.
Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbos is unlike the songs of the other days: on the other days someone sang for the day, but Shabbos sings for itself.
Creation was made with seven notes, one for each day, and only on Shabbos was the harp complete, so Shabbos is the day of song.

summary.en: The Rav opens with the mitzvah to serve Hashem with all one's heart, which Chazal call tefillah. He explains that the Avos instituted the three tefillos, that the karbanos correspond to them, and that the first bracha connects us to the Avos; a tefillah without the heart is not called tefillah.

title.en: Rambam and Ramban; the heart of the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah

summary.en: The Rav brings the machlokes whether there is a daily mitzvah of tefillah or only in a time of trouble, and notes that today the whole world is in trouble. He explains that the nusach was composed by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, who were prophets, and that davening with kavanah means meeting their heart with ours.

title.en: The endless depth of tefillah, and davening without kavanah

summary.en: The Rav compares the levels of kavanah in tefillah to pshat, drush and remez in Torah, and brings the Arizal that every tefillah until Moshiach is different. He then discusses one who davens without kavanah, and why today one does not repeat even the first bracha, the bracha of the Avos.

title.en: Sefer Bereishis, Shabbos and the shevatim

summary.en: The Rav says Sefer Bereishis, like the first bracha, connects us to the Avos. He explains that on Shabbos, the day of avodas Hashem, the twelve middle brachos for bodily needs, which parallel the twelve shevatim, are dropped for one bracha of spiritual requests, going straight to the Avos, and compares this to Yerushalayim.

title.en: Kabbalas Shabbos and the song of the seventh

summary.en: The Rav describes Kabbalas Shabbos: six kapitlach for the six weekdays and then Mizmor Shir LeYom HaShabbos for the seventh, with which Shabbos is accepted. He brings Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer on the pattern of six and a seventh, and explains that unlike the Levi'im's songs of the other days, Shabbos sings for itself.

title.en: The seven-stringed harp: Shabbos, the day of song

summary.en: From the Gemara's harp of seven strings and the seven notes of music, the Rav explains that creation's seven days are seven notes, complete only on Shabbos. He connects this to the seven kolos of Havu LaHashem, to Eretz Yisrael, the Kinneres and David HaMelech as the singing sevenths, and to the added mizmorim of Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Rosh Hashana is the day of Hashem's coronation, that a Jew's joy in the King is his strength in judgment, and connects the Rosh Hashana readings to the danger of Yishmael and to the remembering of the barren, Zion among them.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rosh Hashana as the day of the King's coronation: Hashem was always Master of the world, but there is no king without a people, so each year His kingship is accepted anew, and one who refuses it has no place in the King's world. He asks why the Day of Judgment is a Yom Tov, and answers with the Chasam Sofer's mashal of an imprisoned minister who danced on the king's coronation day and was pardoned for his joy, reading Nechemia's words the same way. The joy must be real. The shofar has two reasons, fear of judgment or praise of the King, and which one a person can live depends on whether he did teshuvah in Elul. Nitzavim teaches standing before Hashem prepared. He then urges responsibility for Klal Yisrael facing the Arabs, explains why the Rosh Hashana reading speaks of Yishmael, and ends with Rosh Hashana as the time when the barren are remembered, Zion the seventh of them.

en: Rosh Hashana is the day Hashem is crowned King; since there is no king without a people, a person's place in the world depends on accepting His kingship.
Following the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains that rejoicing in the King's coronation on the Day of Judgment is itself a Jew's strength in that judgment.
The joy must be genuine, and whether the shofar is heard as praise of the King or as fear of judgment depends on whether one did teshuvah in Elul.
Parshas Nitzavim, read before Rosh Hashana, teaches that one must stand before Hashem prepared, able to sing His praises like the angels.
The Rosh Hashana Torah reading speaks of Yishmael because Tishrei, the month of Ephraim, is the time of the battle against Yishmael.
Rosh Hashana is a time of remembering the barren, and Zion is the seventh barren one who will rejoice in her returning children.

title.en: Rosh Hashana as the King's coronation

summary.en: The Rav explains that besides being the Day of Judgment, Rosh Hashana is the coronation day of the King, since there is no king without a people. One who accepts Hashem's kingship through Torah, mitzvos and good middos is written for life in His world; one who does not has no place in it.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer's mashal of the dancing prisoner

summary.en: The Rav brings Nechemia's words to the returning exiles and asks how the Day of Judgment can be a Yom Tov. He answers with the Chasam Sofer's mashal of a minister in prison who danced on the king's coronation day and was pardoned for rejoicing in the king, and concludes that rejoicing with Hashem is a Jew's strength in judgment.

title.en: Genuine joy and the two reasons for shofar

summary.en: The Rav stresses that the joy must be real, not dancing without rejoicing in Hashem's kingship. He brings Rav Saadia Gaon that the shofar can be fear of judgment or praise of the King, and explains that only one who did teshuvah in Elul can enter Rosh Hashana with a light heart; otherwise the shofar makes him tremble, like the Satan in Tosafos.

title.en: Nitzavim: standing prepared before the King

summary.en: The Rav calls the Rosh Hashana shofar the shofar of the King's coronation, and explains that Parshas Nitzavim is read beforehand to teach standing face to face before Hashem prepared, not in shame. He brings Rabbi Pinchas of Koretz that the praises and piyutim sweeten judgment, and says one who comes with joy can sing before Hashem like the angels.

title.en: Responsibility for Klal Yisrael and the pere adam

summary.en: The Rav tells the bachurim they must feel responsible for Klal Yisrael, which faces great danger from the Arabs, whom he identifies with Yishmael the pere adam, a wild man who stays wild even with education. He asks them to pray that Hashem foil their plans as He foiled Haman's.

title.en: Why the Rosh Hashana reading speaks of Yishmael

summary.en: The Rav asks why, when every Yom Tov's reading is about that Yom Tov, the Rosh Hashana reading is mostly about Yishmael. He answers that Tishrei is the month of Ephraim, whose nasi Elishama bears Yishmael's letters, and is the time of the battle against Yishmael, whose fall will bring Moshiach.

title.en: Remembering the barren, and Zion the seventh

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rosh Hashana, when Sarah was remembered, is a time of remembering the barren, and brings the Midrash of seven barren women, the seventh being Zion. He adds that Hashem Himself blows the shofar and blesses the month for us, includes one whose learning and tefillah bear no fruit, and closes with blessings for a good year.

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows from Chazal, Rashi and stories of tzaddikim how severe it is to shame another Jew, and how far the Torah goes to protect the honor of every person.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with an old mussar sefer: one who shames his friend in public must fast forty days, and today, when nobody can fast, Hashem sends the sincere penitent great mitzvos to repair it. He brings the Gemara that one who shames another publicly loses his share in the World to Come, worse than a murderer, because he does not feel his sin and never repents. Boaz lost his sixty children for not inviting Manoach, even with good intent. Kavod habriyos overrides the Kohen Gadol's Yom Kippur service, forbids steps to the mizbeach, shields the fearful soldier, and even spared Bilam disgrace. After the story of the chol bird, he tells how Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin refused to sign the cherem against the chassidim, and how Rabbi Avraham of Slonim tied his chain of great descendants to this.

en: Shaming another in public is worse than murder in one respect: the murderer knows he sinned and repents, while the one who shames does not feel the gravity of what he did.
Shaming a Jew is forbidden even when it is meant for the sake of Heaven, as Boaz's punishment shows.
Kavod habriyos, human dignity, is so great that burying a met mitzvah overrides even the Kohen Gadol's Yom Kippur service.
If the Torah cares for the honor of unfeeling stones and even of a rasha like Bilam, all the more must every Jew be honored.
Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin refused to sign the cherem against the chassidim, and Rabbi Avraham of Slonim attributed his chain of great descendants to this.

title.en: Forty days of fasting for shaming a friend

summary.en: The Rav cites an old mussar sefer that one who shamed his friend in public must appease him and also fast forty days. Since nobody can fast today, he explains, Hashem sends a sincere penitent great mitzvos to repair the blemish, just as He finds ways for a thief who cannot find his victims.

title.en: Worse than murder; Boaz and Manoach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that one who shames his friend in public has no share in the World to Come, and asks why this is harsher than murder. He then tells the Gemara's account that Boaz lost his sixty children because he never invited Manoach to their weddings, and stresses that a good intention is no excuse for shaming a Jew.

title.en: Kavod habriyos: the met mitzvah and the mizbeach

summary.en: The Rav explains the mitzvah of kavod habriyos, greater still for the dead: a Kohen Gadol on the eve of Yom Kippur who finds a met mitzvah must bury it and lose the Yom Kippur service. He then brings the prohibition of steps to the mizbeach and Rashi's kal vachomer: if the Torah protects the honor of unfeeling stones, how much more a person, so one may not embarrass any Jew, even to teach him a lesson.

title.en: The fearful soldier and Bilam's donkey

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that the newly married man and the one who planted a vineyard are sent home from war so that the one who fears his sins is not shamed when he returns. He then brings Rashi that the angel killed Bilam's donkey so it would not be a disgrace to Bilam, and asks how much more one must honor a Jew.

title.en: The chol bird in Noach's teivah

summary.en: The Rav tells the Midrash of the chol bird that hid in a corner of the teivah rather than trouble the busy Noach for food, and was blessed by Noach to live forever. He connects this to the words 'like the chol' and concludes that one never loses through good middos.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov's path and the Chofetz Chaim

summary.en: The Rav describes the new path of the Ba'al Shem Tov, serving Hashem with love and joy, and the opposition of the great misnagdim led by the Vilna Gaon, while later honest Litvaks came to respect the chassidim. He tells, as he heard from talmidim, how the Chofetz Chaim had two grandsons of the Berditchever Rav admitted to his full yeshivah so they would be in his shul on Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin and the cherem

summary.en: The Rav tells how Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin refused to sign the Vilna Gaon's cherem against the chassidim, answering from the akeidah that to harm a Jew an angel is not enough, though to save one even an angel is obeyed. He brings Rabbi Avraham of Slonim's observation that the greatest leaders left a chain of great descendants, and that among the Litvaks only Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin did, because he would not harm a Jew.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Pinchas acted as a simple member of Klal Yisrael, not above it, and sees the same holiness of the Jewish people in the thousands who searched for a lost child this week, closing with emunah in Hashem's hidden reckoning and the comfort of Parshas Pinchas.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Pinchas, who as a killer should have lost the kehunah yet became a new kohen through his deed. Aharon received kehunah as a gift; Pinchas earned it by atoning for Klal Yisrael. The word 'besocham' shows he did not raise himself above the people: knowing he risked the kehunah, he acted only to sanctify Hashem's name as a simple member of Klal Yisrael, which is why Moshe Rabbeinu, the leader, could not be the one. Zimri was a Jew with a foreign growth attached to him. This week too a Jew fell, while thousands of plain Jews from Boro Park and elsewhere searched all night for a lost child, showing that Jews are merciful, modest and kind. Parshas Pinchas brings comfort before the three weeks, which this rare year it precedes, with the haftorah of Eliyahu. The Rav closes that the reckoning of souls is hidden until Moshiach comes, reads the long Ani Maamin on hashgachah, and calls to be comforted with Shabbos.

en: Aharon received the kehunah as a gift, while Pinchas earned it by atoning for Klal Yisrael, so it passed to his descendants.
'Besocham' teaches that Pinchas did not raise himself above Klal Yisrael; he acted as a simple Jew, a member of the people.
Pinchas knew he risked the kehunah and acted only to sanctify Hashem's name and show that Klal Yisrael has no connection to Zimri.
The thousands of plain Jews who searched all night for a lost child showed what a Jew is: merciful, modest and doing kindness.
Parshas Pinchas, with its moadim and the haftorah of Eliyahu, is a comfort for the Jewish people in the time of the three weeks.
How each soul reaches its tikkun is hidden from us until Moshiach comes; now one must believe that everything was for the good.

From 'besocham' he shows that Pinchas did not set himself above the people but acted as a simple Jew for the sake of kiddush Hashem, which is why Moshe Rabbeinu could not be the one to act.

title.en: Zimri's foreign growth and this week's search

summary.en: The Rav describes Zimri as a Jew to whom something foreign attached itself, and compares a Jew who fell this week. Against that, he describes the thousands of plain Jews who searched all night for a lost child and the kiddush Hashem at the levayah, showing that Jews are merciful, modest and kind.

title.en: Parshas Pinchas as comfort before the three weeks

summary.en: The Rav explains that Parshas Pinchas, with its moadim and Eliyahu, comforts the Jewish people in the three weeks, and notes that this rare year it falls before them. He adds that the moadim correspond to the Avos, and that Eliyahu, whose name equals 'ben', will reveal that Jews are Hashem's children.

title.en: Emunah in Hashem's hidden reckoning; comfort of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav says the tikkun of each soul is a reckoning we cannot grasp until Moshiach comes, and that the child came into the world for his own tikkun. He reads the long version of Ani Maamin on the sufferings of tzaddikim and hashgachah pratis, then closes that this week Klal Yisrael appeared in its glory and one must be comforted with Shabbos.

catalogTitle: A Song Depicting the Harmony of בריאה - the Essence of שבת (Intro. to מזמור שיר ליום השבת)

oneLiner.en: The Rav introduces Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos as the song Shabbos itself sings: the harmony of all of creation, which will be seen in full on the day that is entirely Shabbos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the ten authors of Sefer Tehillim, all included in David HaMelech, the harp of seven strings that will have eight and then ten. He ties ten to the ten utterances of creation and explains that the tenth creation is menuchah, satisfaction, created on Shabbos and also found by a chassan and kallah. He then explains that Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos was David's portion in Torah, sung first by Adam HaRishon when Shabbos pleaded for him, and why Tehillim opens the way for tefillah in Pesukei D'zimra. Asking why the song of Shabbos never mentions Shabbos, he explains that the world was created with seven middos, seven notes; music is their harmonious arrangement. History is such a harmony, though a person sees only a dark patch, like a fly on a painting. Mizmor Shir sings of the day that is entirely Shabbos, when everyone will see the whole picture and have menuchah.

en: Sefer Tehillim has ten authors, matching the ten utterances of creation, yet all of it belongs to David HaMelech, the harp whose strings grow from seven to eight to ten.
The Rav explains that menuchah, the satisfaction of lacking nothing, was itself a creation made on Shabbos, and the bond of chassan and kallah is that same creation.
Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos is David HaMelech's portion in Torah, which Adam HaRishon brought out first, with David's permission, after Shabbos pleaded for him.
Pesukei D'zimra, saying David's Tehillim before davening, cuts a path through the accusers, since David says his words together with the one who says them.
The world was created with seven middos, seven notes, and every event is one of them or a combination; music is their harmonious arrangement, not a random striking of keys.
Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos sings of the day that is entirely Shabbos, when the whole design of history will be seen and the world will have menuchah; the weekly Shabbos is a small taste of it.

title.en: Ten authors, one harp, ten utterances

summary.en: The Rav lists the ten authors of Tehillim and says all of it is David HaMelech's, the harp of seven strings that will have eight with Moshiach and ten later. He links ten to the ten utterances of creation, and brings the Gemara that Bereishis itself is the first utterance containing all the others.

title.en: Menuchah: the creation of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains that the bond of chassan and kallah is a creation called Shabbos, and brings Rashi that what the world lacked was menuchah, which was created on Shabbos. Menuchah means satisfaction; he then explains that Kabbalas Shabbos is made with Bo'i Kallah, and describes its three phases.

title.en: David's portion, sung first by Adam

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew has his portion of chiddushim in Torah, which someone earlier may bring out before its time. Tehillim is David HaMelech's portion, and Adam HaRishon, saved from expulsion when Shabbos pleaded for him, sang Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos with David's permission.

title.en: Why Tehillim clears the way for tefillah

summary.en: The Rav says all yeshuos are in Sefer Tehillim, and explains that Pesukei D'zimra cuts away the accusers who block tefillos from rising. Since David says his words together with the one who says them, his name works like a royal stamp on a letter that the guards must let through.

title.en: The song Shabbos sings, and seven notes

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the Levi'im's daily songs with Shabbos, where the day itself sings, since Shabbos completes the seven strings. He asks why this song never mentions Shabbos, and begins to answer: the world was created with seven middos, one per day, and every event and every sound is one of seven notes.

title.en: Music is harmony; so is history

summary.en: The Rav explains that music is not random notes, like a cat on a piano, but notes arranged to match, which is why a chassan and kallah have music. The world is such a symphony: history fits together toward one purpose, and one who knows everything is for his good feels satisfied.

title.en: The fly on the painting and the great Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains that Mizmor Shir speaks of the past, present and future of the world. Like a fly on a black patch of a masterpiece, people see only the dark part; when Moshiach comes, on the day that is entirely Shabbos, everyone will see the whole design and have menuchah, and the weekly Shabbos is a small reflection of it.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Avraham Avinu, the 'third challah' of the world, left his children the inheritance of emunah, and teaches how to make that emunah clear and how to guard it from the thieves who want to steal it.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Parshas Lech Lecha with a mashal of a woman whose Shabbos challos fail to rise twice and succeed the third time. Adam HaRishon was the 'challah of the world' and did not succeed; neither did the world after Noach; the third challah, Avraham Avinu, succeeded, and from him came the Jewish people. His legacy to his children is emunah, first mentioned in the Torah by him. Every Jew believes, but most have a dim emunah rather than a clear one; clear emunah means knowing that Hashem is here and sees everything, and it grows through Torah, mitzvos and tefillah. Emunah, heard at Sinai from Hashem Himself, is a precious diamond that the yetzer hara wants to steal. The Rav gives three ways to guard it: keep away from apikorsus, do not get caught up in politics as if people run the world, and believe that all Hashem does is good even when one cannot understand, like Avraham at the Akeidah.

en: Adam HaRishon, and then the world of Noach, were 'challos' that did not succeed; Avraham Avinu was the third challah that did, and from him came the Jewish people who will enter the day that is entirely Shabbos.
The inheritance Avraham Avinu gave his children is emunah, and every Jew, even one who claims he does not believe, truly believes.
Most people have emunah that is dim rather than clear; clear emunah means knowing that Hashem is here and sees and knows everything, and it grows with more Torah, mitzvos and tefillah.
Emunah is a precious diamond, heard directly from Hashem at Sinai, and the yetzer hara and his forces try to steal it, or at least a piece of it, so it must be guarded.

The Rav gives three ways of guarding emunah: keeping away from apikorsim, not being drawn into political talk that forgets that Hashem runs the world, and believing that everything Hashem does is for the good.
Avraham's test at the Akeidah was not the sacrifice itself but that he could have had a kushya, and he went with joy to do Hashem's will without looking at it.

candidateTopics: guarding emunah from the yetzer hara

title.en: Avraham Avinu, the third challah of the world

summary.en: The Rav tells a mashal of a woman whose Shabbos challos fail twice and rise the third time, and applies it: Adam HaRishon, the 'challah of the world', and the world after Noach did not succeed, while Avraham Avinu, the third challah, did. Avraham's inheritance to his children is emunah.

title.en: Every Jew believes: dim emunah and clear emunah

summary.en: The Rav says every Jew believes, even one who says he does not, and that the first mention of emunah is by Avraham. He distinguishes dim from clear emunah, which means knowing Hashem is present and watching, and says that clear emunah would keep a person from sinning, so one must work on it.

title.en: Emunah, a diamond that thieves want to steal

summary.en: The Rav calls emunah the most precious diamond, the foundation of all mitzvos, since the first two of the Ten Commandments were heard from Hashem Himself. The yetzer hara and his forces want to steal it, as the Satan took it from Adam and Chava, so emunah must be guarded.

title.en: Guarding emunah: apikorsim and politics

summary.en: The first safeguard is to keep away from even a 'small apikores' and not to argue with him, since such words are poison. The second is not to get caught up in political talk, like the talk about the presidential election, as if the president runs the world; one may daven and make hishtadlus, as for parnassah, but must know that Hashem alone leads the world.

title.en: Believing that all Hashem does is good

summary.en: The third safeguard is to believe that everything Hashem does is for the good. The Rav raises the question of the suffering righteous and the prospering wicked, which Moshe Rabbeinu wanted to understand and which Yirmiyahu asked while declaring Hashem righteous, and explains that a tzaddik may suffer to repair what he damaged in an earlier gilgul. He opens the example of the bondage in Egypt.

title.en: Gilgulim in Egypt and in later decrees

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that the Jews in Egypt were souls of the generation of the flood and of the dispersion, punished measure for measure: bricks and mortar for those who built the tower, the river for those of the flood. He adds that tzaddikim revealed that the victims of the decrees of Tach v'Tat were the biryonim of the Churban, and that today, without ruach hakodesh, one must still know that all is by Hashem's just reckoning.

title.en: The test of the Akeidah: serving despite a kushya

summary.en: The Rav explains that Avraham's test at the Akeidah was not giving up his son, which idol worshippers also did, but serving Hashem with joy despite the kushya that Yitzchak was promised as his heir. A non-Jew can sacrifice but cannot bear a kushya; a Jew knows Hashem is righteous whether or not he understands, and that in the end all will be seen as good.

oneLiner.en: Starting from the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'make a light for the teivah' as making the word of prayer shine, the Rav teaches the bachurim that tefillah, said slowly, aloud and with the whole heart, is the ark that saves a Jew from the flood of this world.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Ba'al Shem Tov on Parshas Noach: the teivah is the word of prayer, which one must fill with light and enter with one's whole being. Through his rebbe he ties this to the plain meaning: the world is a flood of desires, and as Noach was saved by the ark, a Jew is saved by davening, above all a long morning davening. He tells how a camp minyan of bachurim who davened slowly grew into the shul's minyan, and explains with the Gemara why tefillah, though it stands at the height of the world, is mocked. He then reads the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo: the world was created so that people gather in shuls and proclaim aloud that they are His creations, and loud davening overpowers the yetzer hara. From the Ba'al HaTanya's letters he shows the call for slow chazzanim and long davening, and closes that in the time before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah with the whole heart, alongside learning.

en: The Ba'al Shem Tov reads 'make a light for the teivah' as making each word of prayer shine, and 'come into the teivah with all your household' as putting one's whole self into the words.
The world is a flood of desires and pursuit of honor in which most people drown, and as Noach was saved by the ark, a Jew is saved by davening, especially a long morning davening.
According to the Ramban, Hashem created the world so that people gather in shuls and proclaim aloud that they are His creations, which is the purpose of raising the voice in prayer.

The Ba'al HaTanya asks that the weekday chazzan be someone with time, who can daven shacharis for at least an hour and a half, and he is pained by those who push a long-davening chazzan away from the amud.
Davening fast without kavanah fulfills only the rabbinic mitzvah of tefillah, not the Torah mitzvah of serving Hashem with all one's heart.
In the generations before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, though bachurim must still learn all day, since the start of a person's life, like the start of the world, belongs to Torah.
