avodah in the time before Moshiach

title.en: The teivah is the word of prayer

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's reading of 'make a light for the teivah' as filling the word of prayer with light and entering it with everything one has. He asks how this drush fits the plain meaning and answers with his rebbe's teaching that the world is a flood, and as Noach was saved by the ark a Jew is saved by davening, above all in the morning.

title.en: A bachurim minyan, and why prayer is mocked

summary.en: The Rav tells how, as rosh hamasmidim in camp, he organized young bachurim to daven slowly in the morning, and how their request to continue in the city became the minyan of the shul. He then asks why someone who learns well is honored while someone who davens well is mocked, and answers with the Gemara that tefillah is among the things that stand at the height of the world yet people treat lightly.

title.en: The Ramban: prayer is the purpose of creation

summary.en: The Rav explains that reading a holy sefer in the author's own words is as if the author stands before the reader, and then reads the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo. The Ramban writes that the purpose of the mitzvos and of creation is that people recognize Hashem as their Creator, thank Him and turn to Him in prayer.

title.en: Davening aloud, in shul, against the yetzer hara

summary.en: Continuing the Ramban, the Rav explains that shuls and loud prayer exist so that people gather and proclaim before Hashem that they are His creations, and brings the Yerushalmi on the people of Nineveh that prayer needs a voice. He adds that loud davening overpowers the yetzer hara, who urges a quick davening, and brings Reb Aharon of Karlin that simple people must daven aloud, as is the custom in Stolin.

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya's letter on the chazzan

summary.en: The Rav reads a letter of the Ba'al HaTanya asking that working men not lead the weekday davening, but melamdim and kollel yungeleit who can daven shacharis for at least an hour and a half, chosen by lot or by the majority, with the others surrounding the chazzan. He adds that in his shul the best places around the amud are given to the bachurim, who still have freshness in davening.

title.en: Don't drive away the long-davening chazzan

summary.en: From a second letter, the Rav explains why the Ba'al HaTanya was pained by people who push a slow chazzan from the amud: one who lengthens his prayer lengthens his days, and they drive away that life. He tells of the Chasam Sofer's answer to a friend about long davening, and concludes that a person who must hurry to work should rather leave, even without hearing kedushah, than rush the chazzan, applying this to his own yungeleit.

title.en: Prayer with the whole heart before Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that fast davening without kavanah fulfills only the rabbinic mitzvah, not the Torah mitzvah of serving Hashem with all one's heart, and brings the Shulchan Aruch on kavanah in the first berachah. He returns to the Ba'al HaTanya: in the time before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, while bachurim must still learn, and in davening the hidden love of Hashem in every Jew comes out.

catalogTitle: 'טוב להודות לה - Because We See that Everything is Coordinated By Him (פירוש על מזמור שיר פסוק בפסוק)

oneLiner.en: Going through Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos verse by verse, the Rav explains that the psalm is the song of the future eternal Shabbos, when all the questions of history will be answered and it will be clear that everything Hashem did was for the good.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah that calls Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos the song of the day that is entirely Shabbos: the seventh millennium after six thousand years. Menucha, he explains, does not mean rest but satisfaction, the feeling of lacking nothing, and our weekly Shabbos is a small taste of it. In that future time the questions that plague people today will dissolve. He lists the suffering of Jewish history, from the Churban and the Ten Martyrs to the Crusades, the Spanish expulsion and the Holocaust, and shows that tzaddikim knew hidden reasons for some of it. Moshe Rabbeinu himself was not shown why the righteous suffer. The Rav then explains each verse: thanking Hashem also means agreeing with Him, daytime understanding versus nighttime emunah, the happy and sad tunes of history, the flourishing of the wicked, the tzaddik like the palm and cedar, and the missing vav of 'avlasa', the connection we will only see later.

en: Our weekly Shabbos is a small glimpse of the seventh millennium, the 'day that is entirely Shabbos'.
Menucha means satisfaction and gratification, the feeling of lacking nothing, not mere rest.
The suffering of tzaddikim throughout history has reasons that Hashem knows, even when the greatest tzaddikim do not, and in the seventh millennium they will be understood.
When things are clear one thanks Hashem from understanding; in the dark times one must rely on emunah.
Knowing that Hashem is the One doing everything, and that nothing is chance, is itself a source of joy whatever the tune.
In the future the connection between all the events of history will be seen, like the pieces of a puzzle put together.

title.en: Shabbos as a taste of the eternal Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah that Mizmor Shir L'yom HaShabbos is the song for the day that is entirely Shabbos, the seventh millennium, and explains that menucha means satisfaction, not rest, bringing Naomi's words to Ruth and Rashi on the creation's completion. A true Shabbos is kept as if all one's work were done.

title.en: The questions of Jewish suffering

summary.en: In the seventh millennium, the Rav says, there will be no more questions. He lists the troubles that raise questions in emunah: the Churban, the Crusades, the Spanish expulsion and the Holocaust, where precisely tzaddikim suffered, and he tells of the Ten Martyrs and Rabbi Yishmael, who asked Heaven whether to accept the decree.

title.en: Hidden reasons behind the decrees

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Ten Martyrs were a gilgul of the ten tribes, atoning for the sale of Yosef, and that tzaddikim of a later generation said those killed then were a gilgul of the rebels in the Gemara in Gittin who refused Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai's surrender to Rome. For the Holocaust no one today can give the reason, but Hashem knows it.

title.en: Tov l'hodos: thanking and agreeing

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Moshe Rabbeinu asked why the righteous suffer and was not told, and says that in the seventh millennium we will thank Hashem even for the suffering, as Yeshayahu says. He explains 'tov l'hodos' as both thanking and agreeing that Hashem's ways are just, and gives the parable of the fly on a painting.

title.en: Morning understanding, nighttime emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains 'l'hagid baboker chasdecha ve'emunascha baleilos': in times of light one can examine and understand Hashem's kindness, while in the dark times, when tzaddikim suffer and the wicked prosper, one needs emunah. He then explains 'alei asor va'alei navel' as rich and sad tunes, and brings Rav Nachman of Breslov that every person's life is a niggun.

title.en: The song of history and the tailor

summary.en: The Rav says the whole world sings a niggun through the seven millennia, and one must think into the tune history plays. Whatever Hashem does is for our good, like painful surgery, and knowing that He is doing it brings joy. On 'ma gadlu ma'asecha' he tells how someone answered a question after the Holocaust with the parable of a tailor cutting silk.

title.en: Why the wicked flourish

summary.en: On 'ish ba'ar lo yeida' the Rav explains that a mortal cannot understand the Creator, like a watch that cannot understand the watchmaker, and does not even understand that he cannot understand. The wicked flourish only to be destroyed forever, like a turkey being fattened, while Hashem is above and His enemies will be lost.

title.en: The tzaddik's flourishing and the missing vav

summary.en: The Rav explains that the tzaddik will be like both the palm, which gives fruit, and the cedar, which grows tall, and will bear fruit even in old age. The psalm's last verse declares that Hashem is just; the missing vav in 'avlasa', the vav of connection, shows that now we do not see how events connect, but in the future everything will fit together like the Megillah or a puzzle.

oneLiner.en: Through Yosef and his brothers, Tamar and Potifar's wife, a story of the Sanzer Rav and the Midrash on Amalek, the Rav teaches that one must never shame or ruin another Jew, since even a deed meant for the sake of Heaven is wicked without good middos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Yosef sending everyone out before revealing himself, so as not to shame his brothers. He explains that the shevatim, each bound to a combination of Hashem's Name, judged Yosef in beis din as a rodef, and brings the Midrash Tanchuma that some events, like Adam's sin, Moshe's failure at Mei Merivah and the sale of Yosef, had to happen. Yosef therefore risked his life to spare his brothers shame. Rashi says Tamar and Potifar's wife both meant it for the sake of Heaven, yet Potifar's wife is called wicked: Tamar risked her life not to shame Yehuda, while the other had bad middos and libeled Yosef. The Rav applies this to shaming someone who talks during davening, tells of the Sanzer Rav and a business competitor, and explains through a Midrash mashal why Hashem blames Amalek rather than Israel's doubt. He closes with kavod habriyos, love of a Jew as love of Hashem, and a story of the Belzer Rav.

en: Yosef sent everyone out before revealing himself so as not to shame his brothers, even though he thereby put his own life in danger.
The brothers did not act wantonly: they held a beis din and ruled that Yosef had the status of a rodef.
According to the Midrash, certain events were decreed by Hashem and those involved had no real choice, among them the sale of Yosef.
One can act for the sake of Heaven and still be a great rasha if one lacks good middos; the difference between Tamar and Potifar's wife was that Tamar refused to shame Yehuda.
It is no mitzvah to ruin a Jew who is not a tzaddik; rebuke must be given pleasantly and in a friendly way.
Love of a fellow Jew is bound up with love of Hashem, as hinted by the equal gematria of the two verses of 've'ahavta'.

title.en: Yosef spares his brothers shame

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Yosef sent everyone out so his brothers would not be shamed, and explains that the shevatim, each bound to a combination of Hashem's Name, judged Yosef in beis din as a rodef.

title.en: Events Hashem decrees, and Yosef's risk

summary.en: From the Midrash Tanchuma the Rav explains that Adam's sin, Moshe's failure at Mei Merivah and the sale of Yosef had to happen. He then brings the Midrash that Yosef risked being killed by sending everyone out, rather than shame his brothers.

title.en: Tamar and Potifar's wife: middos decide

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Tamar and Potifar's wife both acted for the sake of Heaven, and asks why the latter is called a rasha. He answers that Tamar had good middos and would not shame Yehuda, while Potifar's wife libeled Yosef, and applies this to shaming someone who talks during davening.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav and the competitor

summary.en: The Rav tells of a man in Sanz who claimed it was a mitzvah to ruin a competitor who was not a proper Jew, and of the Sanzer Rav's proof from the darkness in Egypt that it is no mitzvah. He concludes that rebuke must be given pleasantly.

title.en: Amalek and the king's dog

summary.en: The Rav asks why Hashem says 'remember what Amalek did' rather than reminding Israel of their doubt 'is Hashem among us'. He brings the Midrash's mashal of a king whose thieving friend was bitten by the guard dogs, and who blamed the dog so as not to shame his friend.

title.en: Kavod habriyos and love of a Jew

summary.en: The Rav shows the weight of kavod habriyos from the laws of interrupting kerias shema, and brings the remez that the verses of love of Hashem and love of one's fellow are equal in gematria. He mentions the yahrzeit of Rabbi Yissachar Dov of Belz.

title.en: The Belzer Rav's cry on Rosh Hashana

summary.en: The Rav tells of a boy who had strayed and stood outside chatting on Rosh Hashana in Belz, and became a baal teshuvah when he heard the Belzer Rav read 'al er'eh b'mos hayeled' with a cry. He concludes that a word of a tzaddik can break the heart, and one must guard oneself from hearing words against emunah.

title.en: L'chaim and singing

summary.en: The Rav tells the bachurim to make brachos and say l'chaim to their friends, followed by singing.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the war against Midian as a war of holiness against impurity fought with Torah and tefillah, says that today's war against the Jewish people is the same kind of war, and ties the haftarah of Yirmiyahu to the avodah of the Three Weeks.

abstract.en: The Rav begins with the war against Midian in parshas Matos: only tzaddikim were drafted, it had to be led by Moshe Rabbeinu, and for every thousand who fought a thousand stayed back to daven, with the Aron, the Tzitz and the trumpets. Bringing a question of the Satmar Rav, why the Jews stayed pure in Egypt yet fell with Midian, he explains that Bilaam fought with the full power of kishuf and impurity, so the answer had to be a war of holiness. He then says the Torah is eternal: today the Sitra Achra wages that same war, not with the sword but with the tools of impurity, and the answer is Torah and tefillah. Turning to the haftarah, he brings the Chasam Sofer that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, who was a gilgul of Betzalel, and closes with the avodah of the Three Weeks: to turn these days into joy.

en: The war against Midian needed unusual preparations: tzaddikim instead of ordinary soldiers, Moshe Rabbeinu's leadership, a thousand davening for every thousand fighting, and the Aron, Tzitz and trumpets.
Midian did not fight with weapons but with impurity and Bilaam's kishuf, so it was a heavenly war of holiness against impurity.
The Torah is eternal, and today the Jewish people are living through the war of Midian again: a war of impurity rather than of the sword.
Against the tools of kishuf, the Jewish people must come with the holy vessels: the Urim is Torah, and the Tzitz and the trumpets are tefillah.
The avodah of the Three Weeks is to turn these days into joy, so that Yirmiyahu may again become Shlomo HaMelech singing Shir HaShirim in the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: The war of Midian, a war of holiness

summary.en: Following the Nesivos Shalom, the Rav describes the unusual preparations for the war against Midian and brings the Satmar Rav's question why the Jews fell there after staying pure in Egypt. He answers that Bilaam fought with all the forces of kishuf and impurity, so the war had to be fought with holiness, as a last battle before entering Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Today's war of Midian

summary.en: The Rav says the Torah is eternal and that the Jewish people are living through the war of Midian today: not the sword of the long galus but the tools of impurity. The answer is the holy vessels, Torah and tefillah, and parshas Matos read this Shabbos gives strength for this war, which each person fights at his own level.

title.en: Yirmiyahu, Shlomo and the Three Weeks

summary.en: On the haftarah, the Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo HaMelech, and Shlomo of Betzalel, explaining why Betzalel needed the people's consent and why Shlomo had to witness the churban. He closes with the avodah of the Three Weeks: to turn these days into joy, so that Yirmiyahu may again be Shlomo singing Shir HaShirim.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that at his milah Avraham Avinu was remade by Hashem into a new creation who believes in the Ribono shel Olam by nature, and that this emunah passes to his children by inheritance, the way animals inherit instinctive knowledge.

abstract.en: The Rav announces that this year he will speak about emunah, the foundation of all the mitzvos. The Rambam counts 'Anochi Hashem Elokecha' as the mitzvah of emunah, connected to Avraham, the first believer, whose emunah was simple, without chochmah. The Ramban holds that emunah is not one of the 613 but their foundation, like the foundation of a house, and the Rav argues the Ramban seems right, since every mitzvah is phrased as a command while 'Anochi' is a statement. To defend the Rambam he builds a long introduction: bodily features and middos are inherited, learned knowledge is not, yet animals such as the bee, the beaver and the spider are born with knowledge. Avraham was a new creation: at his milah Hashem gave him the letter heh and made him a being who believes instinctively, and he was first made barren to cut him off from Terach. Every Jew inherits this emunah, which raises a question about Jews who deny it, left for next week.

en: The Rambam counts 'Anochi Hashem' as the mitzvah of emunah, while the Ramban holds emunah is not one of the 613 but the foundation on which all of them stand.
Every mitzvah in the Torah is written as a command, while 'Anochi Hashem' is a statement in which Hashem presents Himself, so the Rav says the Ramban appears to be right.
Bodily features and character traits pass from parents to children, but learned knowledge does not; animals, however, are born with knowledge of how to build a hive, a dam or a web.
At his milah Hashem remade Avraham Avinu into a new creation who believes in the Ribono shel Olam by nature, not only through his intellect.
This emunah passes by inheritance to all of Avraham's children, who are therefore believers the sons of believers.

title.en: The mitzvah of emunah and Avraham

summary.en: After a garbled opening, the Rav says that this year he will speak about emunah, the foundation of all the mitzvos. He brings 'Anochi Hashem' as the mitzvah of emunah according to the Rambam and ties it to Avraham Avinu, whose emunah was simple, without chochmah, like that of our grandmothers.

title.en: Rambam and Ramban: is emunah a mitzvah?

summary.en: The Rav presents the Ramban's view that emunah is not one of the 613 mitzvos but their foundation, like the foundation of a house. He argues that the Ramban seems right: every mitzvah is phrased as a command, while 'Anochi Hashem' is a statement, like a doctor introducing himself.

title.en: What a child inherits from his parents

summary.en: To answer for the Rambam the Rav begins a long introduction: features of the body, such as skin color, and traits of the soul, such as a quick temper, are inherited. Knowledge, such as knowing Bava Metzia by heart, is not inherited; it is acquired through toil in learning.

title.en: Inborn knowledge: bee, beaver and spider

summary.en: The Rav shows that there is knowledge that is inherited: the bee builds its precise honeycomb, the beaver builds a dam, and the spider spins its species' web, though none was ever taught. He concludes that such knowledge is part of the creature's very being and passes on by inheritance.

title.en: Avraham Avinu as a new creation

summary.en: The Rav says two things were created after the creation of the world: fire on motzaei Shabbos, and Avraham Avinu, a new creation whose novelty is his knowledge of Hashem. Others are punished for not believing because they could know through contemplating the world but do not want to; Avraham was remade at his milah to believe by nature, and the Rav begins to explain the small heh of 'behibaram' as the letter of birth.

title.en: The heh of birth and Avraham's new name

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world was completed when Avraham received the heh at his bris. He shows the heh as the letter of birth from Rachel, whose name lacks a heh, from a segulah of a silver heh, and from 'hei lachem zera', and brings the verses in davening about Avraham's new name and his faithful heart: the new thing in him, emunah, passes to his children.

title.en: Cut off from Terach; a question for next week

summary.en: The Rav explains that Avraham was created barren to sever him from the generations of Terach, so that a new people believing in Hashem would begin from him, and he brings Rashi on why Terach's death is written before Avraham leaves. He ends with a strong question: if every Jew inherits emunah, how can there be Jews who deny Hashem? The answer is left for next week.

catalogTitle: 'להגיד כי ישר ה - An Explanation to all our Hardships (Added insights on מזמור שיר)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains how Mizmor Shir l'Yom haShabbos, culminating in 'lehagid ki yashar Hashem', teaches that in the Yom shekulo Shabbos every hardship, even the harshest Midas haDin, will be seen as chesed.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the question of tzaddik v'ra lo that Yirmiyahu raised, and answers that the world was meant to be run by Midas haDin, which today we cannot bear; in the Yom shekulo Shabbos we will see that it was all chesed. He explains the psalm's contrast between the wicked, who sprout like grass and wither, and the tzaddik, who grows slowly like the date palm and the cedar, and shows how the Jewish people outlived Egypt, Bavel, Rome and Greece. He brings the Hafla'ah's reading of the palm and the cedar, Chanoch and Avraham Avinu, and a tangent on good company. Returning to the psalm, he concludes that Hashem is straight. Through the Arizal's combinations of the Shem Havaya for each month, the order of male and female, right and left, he shows that even Tammuz, the Shem backwards, will be revealed as chesed.

en: The Rav explains that the world was meant to run by Midas haDin, which people cannot bear today because everyone sins, but in the Yom shekulo Shabbos it will be revealed as chesed.
The wicked flourish quickly like grass and wither, while the tzaddik grows slowly like the date palm and the cedar and endures.
The Jewish people, like the date palm, have outlived all their oppressors: Egypt, Bavel, Rome and Greece.
'Lehagid ki yashar Hashem' means that one day it will be seen that everything Hashem did was straight and for our good.
Each month has its own combination of the Shem Havaya; where the male letters come first it is chesed, and where the order is reversed it is din.
Even Tammuz, where the Shem Havaya is completely backwards and at the ends of the words, will be revealed as straight and chesed.

title.en: Why tzaddikim suffer: Midas haDin

summary.en: The Rav recalls that the psalm's theme is the Yom shekulo Shabbos and brings Yirmiyahu's complaint about tzaddik v'ra lo. He explains that the world was meant to be run by Midas haDin, that today we cannot bear it, and that later we will understand all past suffering as chesed.

title.en: Grass and the date palm

summary.en: The Rav explains why the wicked bloom like grass, quickly and briefly, while the tzaddik grows like the date palm and the cedar. He applies it to the Jewish people, who outlived Egypt, Bavel, Rome, England's ancient people and Greece, and mentions Jews in the camps singing that they would outlive their murderers.

title.en: The palm, the cedar, Chanoch and Avraham

summary.en: The Rav brings the Hafla'ah: the palm gives its strength to its fruit and stays short, while the cedar bears none and grows tall. He contrasts Chanoch, who isolated himself and became a malach, with Avraham Avinu, who taught others, and explains the promise that one who gives his time to talmidim will still grow like the cedar.

title.en: Planted in Hashem's house: good company

summary.en: On 'shesulim b'veis Hashem' the Rav asks why Yaakov struggled to leave the womb when a malach was teaching him Torah, and answers that being with Esav outweighed having such a rebbe, since friends matter more than the rebbe. He brings the Rambam on how strongly one's surroundings shape a person.

title.en: Lehagid ki yashar Hashem

summary.en: Returning to the psalm, the Rav explains that tzaddikim bear fruit even in old age and will live forever in the Yom shekulo Shabbos. The psalm tells us not to look at the present: then we will see that every trouble was for our good, and its purpose is to proclaim that Hashem is straight.

title.en: The month's combination of the Shem Havaya

summary.en: Turning to Musaf of Rosh Chodesh, the Rav explains the Arizal's teaching that each month has its own combination of the Shem Havaya, drawn from a passuk, as with Nisan and Iyar. He explains that male is chesed and the giver, female is din and the receiver, and that Yaakov's sons came before the daughters while by Esav the reverse.

title.en: Right over left, chesed over din

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jew places right over left, chesed over din, as in putting on the right sleeve first, while Esav is din. He brings the Zohar that Avraham had Yishmael and Yitzchak had Esav first to purge bad chesed and bad din, and contrasts the European way of left first, 'ladies first' and writing from the left.

title.en: Tammuz too is chesed

summary.en: The Rav shows how each month's combination fits its climate: Nisan's straight Shem is chesed, Tammuz's reversed Shem is harsh din, and Tishrei and Teves fall in between. Tammuz is the peak of din, the Shem backwards and at the ends of the words, yet 'lehagid ki yashar Hashem' means that even it will be seen as chesed, and what we see now is an optical illusion.

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches bachurim, from a letter of the Ba'al HaTanya, why a tzibbur should daven aloud, together and word by word around a fitting chazan.

abstract.en: Continuing last week's talk on tefillah, the Rav recalls the Ramban that the world was created so that Jews should daven and proclaim aloud that they are Hashem's creations, and the Ba'al HaTanya's call to daven aloud around the chazan. He then reads a letter in which the Ba'al HaTanya begs his chassidim to daven together, word by word, as Klal Yisroel sang the Shirah at the sea. To explain why, he shows that every word of davening carries great depth: lashon hakodesh is Hashem's language, tzaddikim speak a holy language others cannot follow, as a story of the Sanzer Rav and the Ruzhiner shows, and the Chasam Sofer brings from the Ba'al Shem Tov that every word is a heichal. He discusses who should go to the amud, the Ba'al HaTanya's takanos for chazanim, why the crowd and chazan strengthen each other like the angels, answers objections to loud davening, and closes with a story of R' Aharon of Karlin and a call to daven aloud with nusach without disturbing others.

en: The Rav brings the Ramban that the world was created so that Jews should daven and proclaim aloud that they are Hashem's creations.
The Ba'al HaTanya asks that the whole tzibbur daven together, saying each word at the same time, not one here and one there.
Every word of davening is a heichal above, so when all say the same word together the whole tzibbur stands in one heichal.
The amud is not ownerless; the chazan must be someone who can daven with geshmak and nusach and lift up the tzibbur.
When the crowd davens aloud it strengthens the chazan and his loud davening strengthens them, as the angels receive from one another.
One should daven aloud with the tzibbur and its nusach, but not shout off-tune in a way that disturbs others.

title.en: Davening aloud and together

summary.en: The Rav recalls last week's Ramban and Tanya on davening aloud around the chazan, then reads a letter of the Ba'al HaTanya begging his chassidim to daven together word by word, as Klal Yisroel sang the Shirah at the sea.

title.en: The holy language of tzaddikim

summary.en: He explains that every word of davening has great depth: lashon hakodesh is Hashem's language, as Yosef told his brothers, and tzaddikim speak in a holy language others cannot follow, shown by a story of the Sanzer Rav's visit to the Ruzhiner.

title.en: Every word is a heichal

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer quoting the Ba'al Shem Tov that every word of davening is a heichal, and explains that this is why the Ba'al HaTanya wants all to say each word together; he criticizes latecomers and talking or silence during davening.

title.en: Who should go to the amud

summary.en: Following the Ba'al HaTanya, the Rav says the amud is not ownerless: only one who can daven with nusach and geshmak and lift up the tzibbur should go, even on a yahrzeit, and he tells the bachurim to remember this when they are older.

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya's takanos for chazanim

summary.en: The Rav reads the Ba'al HaTanya's advice to appoint set, fitting chazanim who daven word by word aloud without rushing, a weekday davening of about an hour and a half, and his cry of 'gevald' over chazanim who rush.

title.en: Gathering around the chazan, like the angels

summary.en: He explains why the tzibbur gathers around the chazan: the loud crowd and the chazan strengthen each other, as the angels receive from one another and as the Shirah was sung together; he answers those who object to loud davening with a comparison to the shouting at a baseball game and calls for a good eye toward others.

title.en: R' Aharon of Karlin and davening with nusach

summary.en: The Rav tells of R' Aharon of Karlin, whose loud davening brought him before a beis din, and concludes that one should daven aloud with the tzibbur and its nusach, while someone without a good voice should not shout and disturb others.

oneLiner.en: The Rav speaks to bachurim about the danger of jealousy and of shaming another person, through Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah, the story of Kayin and a series of stories of tzaddikim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the line in Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah asking to be saved from jealousy, which he calls the hardest thing in the world and common at every age. He traces kinah from creation: the moon envied the sun, the nachash envied Adam, and Kayin, a great man to whom Hashem spoke, killed Hevel out of envy. Through the Midrash on 'Am I my brother's keeper?' he shows Kayin blaming Hashem for the trait. Kinah led to the sale of Yosef and the churban. He tells bachurim to say that part of the tefillah many times. He then turns to bein adam lachaveiro: the Chernobyler who protected a thief from shame, the Berditchever on the matzah bakers' widows, and the Chasam Sofer's responsum about reburying Reb Mordechai Banet, who was penalized for shaming a kallah though he was right. Reb Shlomo Bloch's story of a young ilui who shamed a rav, and Reb Hershele Rimanover's story with the Yeshuos Yaakov, close the shiur.

en: Kinah is the hardest trait in the world; it is found at every age and even among tzaddikim, and it goes back to creation.
Kayin was a great man, yet jealousy brought him to kill his brother; jealousy also caused the sale of Yosef and, with sinas chinam, the churban.
Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah asks to see the virtues of one's friends and not their faults, and the Rav tells a bachur struggling with jealousy to say it many times.
Good middos between man and his fellow include taking great care never to shame another person.
Even when a person is right, shaming someone carries a heavy price, as with Reb Mordechai Banet and the young ilui.
One who is careful with the honor of others merits all the blessings.

title.en: Kinah from creation to Kayin

summary.en: The Rav opens with the plea against jealousy in Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah, calls kinah the hardest thing in the world, and traces it from the moon and the sun through the nachash to Kayin, a great man to whom Hashem spoke before and after he killed Hevel.

title.en: Kayin's complaint and Rebbe Elimelech's tefillah

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the cheder translation of 'Am I my brother's keeper?' with the Midrash, where Kayin asks Hashem why He gave him such jealousy. He shows kinah behind the sale of Yosef and the churban, explains Rebbe Elimelech's plea to see others' virtues, tells bachurim to say it many times, and tells how Reb Aharon Roth praised the Vizhnitzer Rebbe for being free of jealousy.

title.en: The Chernobyler's spoon and the Berditchever's matzos

summary.en: Turning to good middos between man and his fellow, the Rav tells how the Chernobyler said he gave a stolen silver spoon to a poor man rather than shame him, and how the Berditchever Rav warned the matzah bakers not to put the blood of the overworked widows into their matzos.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer and Reb Mordechai Banet's grave

summary.en: The Rav tells the story behind a responsum of the Chasam Sofer about reburying Reb Mordechai Banet, the Rav of Nikolsburg. The ruling waited six months because Reb Mordechai Banet came to him in a dream: he had to lie six months beside a kallah he had shamed by breaking off a shidduch, though he had been right al pi halachah.

title.en: The ilui who shamed a rav

summary.en: The Rav tells Reb Shlomo Bloch's story of a seventeen-year-old ilui who refuted a visiting rav's pilpul in public and shamed him; he grew into a gadol but never had children, which Reb Shlomo Bloch called his punishment. The Rav concludes that care for the honor of others brings all blessings.

title.en: Reb Hershele Rimanover and the Yeshuos Yaakov

summary.en: The Rav tells how Reb Hershele, a tailor's son, became the shamash and then the successor of Reb Mendel of Rimanov, and how the Yeshuos Yaakov, who would not honor him, removed the chairs, until Reb Hershele stopped at the doorway and the mezuzah was found to be pasul.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why a rotzeach (killer) is sent to the cities of the Levi'im: every life is a song to Hashem, the killer cut off another's song, and the Levi'im, masters of song, reawaken his life, as Shabbos does for every Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Shem MiShmuel in the name of his father, the Avnei Nezer: a killer took life from another, so life is taken from him, and he must go to the cities of the Levi'im so that they can give him life again. To explain this, the Rav teaches that all of creation sings to Hashem with the seven 'voices' of Tehillim 29, and that a person's life itself is his song. The killer cut off another Jew's song, so his own song falls silent, like the sun that Yehoshua stopped. The Levi'im's song is tuned to every Jewish soul, as a tuning fork sets off a piano and as the north wind played David's harp at midnight, and so it reawakens the killer. Every sin holds something of killing, and Shabbos, when Gan Eden comes down, is a city of refuge that makes every Jewish heart sing, above all on the Shabbosos of the Three Weeks.

en: Following the Avnei Nezer, a killer took life from another, so life is taken from him, and the Levi'im must give him life again.
All of creation sings to Hashem with seven voices, and each person's life is his own song.
The killer cut off another's song, so his own song is silenced, like the sun at Givon.
The song of the Levi'im is tuned to every Jewish soul and so it can reawaken the killer's life.
Shabbos, when Gan Eden comes down to the world, is a city of refuge for every sinner and makes every Jewish heart sing.

title.en: The killer and the song of life

summary.en: The Rav brings the Avnei Nezer that a killer must go to the cities of the Levi'im to receive life from them, and begins to explain it: all of creation sings to Hashem with the seven voices, and a person's life is his song, which the killer cut off.

title.en: The silenced sun and the Levi'im's song

summary.en: The Rav compares the killer to the sun that Yehoshua silenced, explains that the Levi'im are the masters of song, and uses a tuning fork and David's harp that played by itself at midnight to show how the Levi'im's song reawakens the killer's soul.

title.en: Shabbos as the city of refuge

summary.en: The Rav explains that on Shabbos Gan Eden comes down and every Jewish heart sings, that Kabbalas Shabbos completes the seven voices, and that Shabbos is a city of refuge for every sin; he ends with the special greatness of the Shabbosos of the Three Weeks.

catalogTitle: Hashem has Always Reigned Supreme (ה' מלך גאות לבש)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the mizmor Hashem Malach Ge'us Lavesh as the song that will be sung in the days of Moshiach, when Klal Yisrael looks back and sees that Hashem reigned throughout the long galus, even when His rule was doubly hidden.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by tying Hashem Malach to the preceding mizmor of Shabbos, whose message is patience: waiting is a tikkun for Adam HaRishon, who did not wait for Shabbos, and for the Yidden at Mattan Torah and Shaul HaMelech, who also did not wait. He then contrasts Hashem Melech, Hashem Yimloch and Hashem Malach: in the days of Moshiach Klal Yisrael will look back and see that Hashem always reigned. Ge'us lavesh, written with lavesh twice, describes a double concealment, illustrated by a child who does not even know his father is near. Hashem girded Himself with strength like a surgeon operating on his own child. Through the Rashi on the Dor Haflagah, the meaning of Tevel, the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of the breeze, the rising rivers and the breakers of the sea, he shows that the world is not falling apart. He ends with the trustworthy Nevi'im and the galus as a march toward the Geulah.

en: Hashem Malach continues the mizmor of Shabbos, whose theme is that Klal Yisrael must wait patiently for the Yom Shekulo Shabbos.

Hashem Melech, Hashem Yimloch and Hashem Malach describe three periods: open prosperity, the galus when Hashem's reign is awaited, and the days of Moshiach when it becomes clear that He always reigned.
The double 'lavesh' points to a concealment that is itself concealed, which is why so many fall away in galus.
Hashem conducts the world for the sake of Klal Yisrael, its purpose, so the world will not fall apart even when it seems to.
The nations, compared to rivers and to the breakers of the sea, rise up against Klal Yisrael, but Hashem is mightier than all of them and they will lament their downfall.
In galus Klal Yisrael is comforted by its emunah in the trustworthy Nevi'im, and its journey through galus is a march toward the Geulah.

title.en: Waiting as a tikkun for Adam's sin

summary.en: The Rav shows that Hashem Malach continues the mizmor of Shabbos, whose message is that Klal Yisrael must wait. He explains that waiting repairs the sin of Adam HaRishon, who did not wait for Shabbos to make kiddush, and brings the Yidden at Mattan Torah and Shaul HaMelech, who also failed to wait.

title.en: Hashem Melech, Yimloch and Malach

summary.en: The Rav explains the three tenses of Hashem's kingship as three periods, and says that in the days of Moshiach Klal Yisrael will look back and proclaim Hashem Malach, that He reigned even in galus. He then explains ge'us lavesh: it seems as if Hashem has withdrawn from caring for this low world.

title.en: Lavesh twice: a hidden concealment

summary.en: The Rav explains why lavesh is written twice through the pasuk of the double hiding, and a parable of a child facing a tiger who does not even know his father is nearby. He concludes that from the vantage point of the days of Moshiach all the pieces will fit together and show that Hashem always reigned.

title.en: Oz his'azar and the fear of collapse

summary.en: The Rav explains oz his'azar with a surgeon who must operate on his own child, and says Hashem conducts the world for Klal Yisrael. He contrasts this with the nations' fear that the world is collapsing, from the Dor Haflagah in Rashi to modern worries, and says the world will not fall apart.

title.en: Tevel: the blurred world

summary.en: The Rav explains the name Tevel as a mixture, a blurred view of the world like astigmatism, and compares the non-believer's world to a dark night lit only by flashes of lightning. He brings the pasuk from Hallel that Hashem, high above the heavens, lowers Himself to watch over the smallest thing on earth.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov's breeze and the hidden throne

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov explained a breeze as sent for one suffering worm, showing that Hashem provides for everything. He then explains nachon kis'acha me'az: Hashem's throne has always been firm, and me'olam relates to concealment, for Hashem governs the world from behind the cracks.

title.en: The rivers and the breakers of the sea

summary.en: The Rav explains that the rivers are the kingdoms of the nations and the breakers of the sea are the great empires, who arrogantly proclaim they will destroy Klal Yisrael. He reads dochyam as their future lament over their own downfall, since Hashem on high is mightier than them all.

title.en: The trustworthy Nevi'im and the march to Geulah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Nevi'im are Hashem's trustworthy witnesses, and in the galus of Hashem Yimloch Klal Yisrael is comforted by emunah in them. Wherever a Yid goes in galus, he says, he is marching toward the Beis HaMikdash and the Geulah, and Hashem and Klal Yisrael are forever.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's emunah is a feeling of the heart inherited from the mother, so that even a Jew who denies Hashem is only rationalizing what he knows deep inside.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by contrasting a gentile, who can grasp emunah through logic, with a Jew, who feels it by instinct. He illustrates with the halacha of a burglar: a son may not kill his father who breaks in, because a father's heart feels for his son even when he does not know whose house it is. From there he distinguishes chochmah, fixed facts that all agree on, from binah, the understanding of the heart, which Chazal say was given more to women; the seder's three matzos and four cups reflect this. Jewishness follows the mother because emunah is a feeling, and he shows from Hebrew grammar that the root of emunah yields the word for mother. He then describes how people rationalize out of pride, from the fox and the grapes, Eisav and a bochur blaming his rebbe, and concludes that a Jewish apikores really believes but denies out of desire, illustrated by a letter written after the Six Day War.

en: A gentile can understand emunah with logic, but a Jew feels it instinctively in his heart.
Chochmah is fixed knowledge all must accept, while binah is the heart's understanding, which differs from person to person according to his nature.
A child's Jewishness follows the mother because emunah is a feeling, and feeling comes from the mother.
A person's pride drives him to justify himself and blame anything but himself, which psychology calls rationalization and denial.
A Jewish apikores truly believes; he denies only because he wants to follow his desires.

title.en: Emunah as instinct: the father and the burglar

summary.en: The Rav opens by saying a Jew feels emunah instinctively, unlike a gentile who reaches it through logic. He brings the halacha of a burglar who may be killed, and Rashi's case of a father breaking in to his son, and argues that even a father who does not know it is his son's house feels it in his heart, as even wild animals do for their young.

title.en: Chochmah and binah, matzos and cups

summary.en: The Rav explains that Jews are Hashem's children and feel bound to Him with the heart, not only the mind. He contrasts chochmah, objective facts, with binah, the heart's understanding, reads 'aliba d'Abaye' as 'according to Abaye's heart', and brings the Gemara that women were given extra binah. The three matzos (grain, intellect) and four cups (wine, feeling) at the seder, matching the Avos and Imahos, show the two sides.

title.en: A wife's feeling and the Lechovitcher's cry

summary.en: The Rav brings the Avnei Nezer's explanation of why a woman may remarry on one witness's word: she feels whether her husband is alive. He then tells how Reb Mordechai of Lechovitch cried out that he no longer felt his Rebbe, Reb Shlomo of Karlin, until he was told the Rebbe had passed away.

title.en: Why Jewishness follows the mother: emunah and em

summary.en: The Rav asks why a child's Jewishness follows the mother when tribe and inheritance follow the father, and answers that emunah is a feeling, which comes from the mother. He supports this from a rule of Hebrew grammar: a three-letter verb ending in nun drops it as a noun (chanan to chen, shanan to shen, ganan to gan), so from aman, to believe, comes em, mother.

title.en: Ben Sira's fox and the sour grapes

summary.en: The Rav mentions the Gemara on outside books, among them Ben Sira's fables, which the gentiles adopted as Aesop's fables. He tells the fable of the fox who could not climb the fence to the grapes and declared them sour, and explains that like every proud person the fox cannot admit his own weakness.

title.en: Eisav, the hammer and the bochur: rationalization

summary.en: The Rav says that everything, even psychology, can be learned from Chumash and Rashi, and shows it with Eisav: seeing that his Canaanite wives displeased his parents, he concluded he lost the berachos because of his wives and married Yishmael's daughter. He adds the man who hits his thumb and blames the hammer and the bochur who blames his rebbe and classroom, calling this rationalization born of pride.

title.en: The Jewish apikores really believes

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jewish apikores denies Hashem only because he wants to follow his desires, cites a philosopher's essay that there never was a true atheist, and tells of the miracles of the Six Day War and a woman who wrote to a newspaper asking it to stop reporting them so she could keep going to the beach on Shabbos. He concludes that every Jew believes.

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches the bachurim that coming early and acting with zerizus shows that the avodah is precious to a person, opens the gates of Heaven for him, and is the special task of the last generation before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a letter of Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz, who wrote that his true portion from all his toil was the time he stood before Hashem in tefillah, even as others laughed at how long he davened. He asks why a giant in learning would say this, and answers that davening is dveykus, closeness to Hashem, and urges davening together with the tzibbur. He then brings the Gemara at the end of Sukkah about the mishmar of Bilgah, whose window in the Beis Hamikdash was closed because they came late, and explains that lateness shows the avodah is not precious to a person, so Heaven closes its gates to him. Applying this to the Bnei Dan, who lagged behind the camp and were struck by Amalek, he says our generation, the last, must repair their flaw with zerizus, which hastens Moshiach. He ends with the souls that came to the Chiddushei HaRim on erev Shabbos, one of them too late.

en: Davening is dveykus, a person's direct closeness to Hashem, which is why Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz called his time in tefillah his true portion.
Coming late shows that the avodah is not precious to a person, as the Gemara shows with the mishmar of Bilgah.
Whoever is late loses his flow of blessing from Heaven, while one who comes early finds the gates of Torah and tefillah opened for him.
Our generation corresponds to the Bnei Dan at the rear of the camp, and its task is to repair their lack of zerizus.
Each Jew has a mitzvah that is the root of his soul, recognized by his desire for it and by the obstacles that block it.
Zerizus in davening and learning can bring Moshiach sooner.

the root mitzvah of each soul
tikkun of souls on erev Shabbos

title.en: Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz's portion in tefillah

summary.en: The Rav brings a letter of Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz, printed in Yaaros Devash, telling a student that while he was still davening, the tzibbur was already done and young people laughed at him, yet this was his portion from all his toil. He asks how a giant in Torah could say his portion was tefillah rather than learning.

title.en: Davening is dveykus; davening together

summary.en: The Rav explains that the mitzvos are counsels for coming close to Hashem, that learning demands concentration on the sugya while davening is dveykus, as the Shulchan Aruch HaRav allows one who has learned much to devote time to dveykus. He describes davening in Stolin and among Sefardim, all together like the angels, and repeats that one should daven together with the tzibbur.

title.en: The mishmar of Bilgah came late

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara at the end of Sukkah: each of the twenty-four mishmaros had its own window for its vessels, and Bilgah's was closed because they came late, so they had to borrow vessels. He explains that coming late shows the avodah is not precious to them, just as bachurim late for davening are on time for a trip.

title.en: A closed window, a closed heart

summary.en: The Rav explains the punishment: whoever comes late shows the avodah is not dear to him, so Heaven closes his flow of blessing, while for one who comes early the gates of Torah and tefillah open. What is in Heaven is in man; a closed heart is a closed window, and a bachur who comes late should make a cheshbon hanefesh and warm himself with mussar and Chassidus.

title.en: The Bnei Dan and our generation

summary.en: The Rav describes how the stragglers of Dan, slow to pack when the camp moved, fell outside the clouds of glory and were attacked by Amalek. Since the camp in space is also a camp in time, the generation of Moshe Rabbeinu is the front and the generation of Moshiach is Dan at the rear, so we must repair their lack of zerizus.

title.en: Each soul's mitzvah and zerizus for Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the rule that every Jew has a mitzvah that is his soul's root, recognized by his desire for it and by the difficulties the yetzer hara puts in its way, and that every generation has such a mitzvah too, as with tzitzis. Our generation's is emunah and zerizus: the Gemara on 'b'itah achishena' shows Moshiach can come sooner, and Amalek, who 'cooled' Israel on the way, is answered with warmth and zerizus.

title.en: The soul that came late on erev Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav tells how souls came to the Chiddushei HaRim on erev Shabbos for a tikkun, and once he told a soul it was too late, since the Rebbetzin had already lit candles. He explains that a soul which was slow in life arrives late after life too, and closes that our generation's task is to be mezarez in Torah and tefillah and bring Moshiach.

catalogTitle: Purify Your נשמה Before Entering שבת (Intro. and beginning of מזמור לדוד הבו)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Mizmor LeDavid, the opening of Kabbalas Shabbos, as the completed harp of seven voices and as the border crossing into Shabbos, where a Jew must purify himself to be let in.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the two customs from Tzfas, the Ramak's Lechu Neranenah and the Arizal's Mizmor LeDavid, both now said, and explains that Mizmor LeDavid begins receiving the extra soul of Shabbos. Its three 'havu' and seven 'kol' match the ten utterances of creation: three upper levels and seven days of time. The seven voices are the seven notes; joined in harmony they make music, mismatched they are noise, and he contrasts holy Jewish music with music that arouses the animal in man. On the seventh day the harp is complete, so we begin to sing. He brings the Gemara that the eighteen names of Hashem in this psalm correspond to Shemoneh Esrei and its seven voices to the Shabbos Shemoneh Esrei. Finally, Mizmor LeDavid is the customs post between the weekday and Shabbos: one must do teshuvah and immerse, as one immerses to enter the Mikdash or Eretz Yisrael, or Shabbos will feel like a burden.

en: The Ramak's custom of opening Shabbos with Lechu Neranenah and the Arizal's of opening with Mizmor LeDavid were both accepted, and with Mizmor LeDavid one begins to receive the extra soul of Shabbos.
The three 'havu' and seven 'kol' of the psalm correspond to the ten utterances of creation: three upper levels beyond time and seven that became the days of the week.
The seven voices are seven notes: matched in harmony they are music, unmatched they are noise, and the Rav contrasts holy Jewish music with music that brings out the animal in man.
The eighteen names of Hashem in Mizmor LeDavid are the eighteen brachos of Shemoneh Esrei, so on Shabbos one does not lose their blessing by not asking for one's needs.
Mizmor LeDavid is the customs post between the weekday and Shabbos, where the angels inspect whether a Jew comes with Torah, mitzvos and teshuvah.
Entering Shabbos requires purification through teshuvah and immersion, and someone who did not prepare is turned away and finds Shabbos a burden.

candidateTopics: seven voices and the seven notes
shemoneh esrei and the eighteen names

title.en: Opening Shabbos with Mizmor LeDavid

summary.en: The Rav describes the Ramak's custom of Lechu Neranenah and the Arizal's of Mizmor LeDavid, and says Mizmor LeDavid starts the receiving of the extra soul of Shabbos. He then ties the psalm's three 'havu' and seven 'kol' to the ten utterances of creation and the seven days.

title.en: Seven voices as notes: harmony and noise

summary.en: The Rav explains that the seven voices appear as the seven notes, which make music only when they match, like colors in a painting or a good shidduch. He contrasts holy Jewish music sung by tzaddikim and at Shabbos zemiros with music whose mismatched noise arouses the animal in man.

title.en: The harp is complete: we begin to sing

summary.en: On the seventh day the harp of seven notes is complete, so Kabbalas Shabbos begins with song; Lecha Dodi adds the Kallah, Malchus, and the Zohar speaks of the union of Shabbos. The Rav notes that he blends what he took from sefarim with his own thoughts, and returns to the three 'havu' and seven 'kol' that together make ten.

title.en: Eighteen names, eighteen brachos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Berachos that the eighteen brachos of Shemoneh Esrei correspond to the eighteen names of Hashem in Mizmor LeDavid and the seven of Shabbos to its seven voices, and tells how the nineteenth bracha was added against the heretics. He concludes that on Shabbos one keeps the blessing of all eighteen brachos by resting and asking only for holy needs.

title.en: Crossing the border into Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav describes entering Shabbos as passing from the domain of the many, the sitra achra, into the domain of the One, and explains why the second day of creation lacks 'ki tov'. Mizmor LeDavid is the customs post where angels inspect a Jew, and just as one immerses to enter the Mikdash or Eretz Yisrael, one immerses to enter Shabbos.

title.en: A mikvah makes a better Jew

summary.en: The Rav tells how a great man saw Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld going to the mikvah daily and heard from him that if a mikvah can make a gentile into a Jew, it can make a Jew into a better Jew. He adds that a gentile may not keep Shabbos, so a Jew must rid himself of the bit of the gentile in him before Shabbos.

title.en: Turned away at the border: preparing for Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav tells of bochurim for whom Shabbos was the hardest day, and explains that they were refused entry for lack of preparation. He says the whole week should prepare for Shabbos, reads 'Kol Hashem al hamayim' as the customs officer's first question, 'did you go to the mikvah?', and stresses that immersion without teshuvah does not help.

oneLiner.en: Through a chain of true stories about gedolim, the Rav shows bachurim how grave it is to shame another Jew and how far great people went to spare others even a moment of distress.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by stressing that the stories he tells come from reliable sources. He tells of a brilliant Slabodka bachur who publicly exposed a friend's borrowed chiddush and, though he became a gadol, died childless; the mashgiach there saw it as punishment for shaming another. He then tells of a soul that came to Reb Moshe of Savran for a tikkun because its owner had shamed a chassan before his father-in-law. A series of stories about Reb Akiva Eiger follows: honoring the Rav of Lissa, hiding his greatness during another chassan's sheva brachos, spilling his own wine to cover a guest's mishap, and conceding a kashya to Reb Mordechai Benet in Nikolsburg. The shiur closes with Reb Yisrael Salanter: his call to account for rabbanim who did not teach middos, his view on asking forgiveness for lashon hara, and his shortening of a Shabbos meal for the sake of a tired maid.

en: The Rav says that shaming another Jew in public is so grave that Chazal say such a person has no share in the World to Come, and the punishment can follow a person all his life.
He warns that young bachurim in particular must be very careful, because they do not yet grasp the severity of shaming another.
Even a correction that seems harmless, made in front of someone's father-in-law, can keep a soul out of Gan Eden.
Reb Akiva Eiger repeatedly gave up his own honor, even letting himself look unlearned, so that no one else would feel slighted.
The Rav says it is better to suffer, even to throw oneself into a fiery furnace, than to shame another.
Reb Yisrael Salanter taught that sensitivity to others, such as a tired maid, comes before extra zemiros and divrei Torah at one's own table.

title.en: The Slabodka bachur who exposed a stolen chiddush

summary.en: The Rav stresses that his stories come from reliable sources, then tells of a brilliant Slabodka bachur who bought copies of a sefer in Vilna to prove publicly that a rival's chiddush was copied. The mashgiach was deeply pained; the bachur became a gadol but died childless, and the Rav warns bachurim to be very careful not to shame anyone.

title.en: A soul punished for shaming a chassan

summary.en: Reb Moshe of Savran told of a soul, a talmid chacham who had done teshuvah, kept out of Gan Eden because he had corrected a chassan's mistaken word in shul in front of his father-in-law. Along the way the Rav tells how his own rebbe, Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz, once corrected an old man's reading in shul and the man became angry.

title.en: Reb Akiva Eiger hides his greatness

summary.en: Reb Akiva Eiger asks the Rav of Lissa to forgive him for receiving the more honored aliyah in Posen. Then, as a young chassan, he gives only simple divrei Torah for a whole Shabbos, nearly losing his shidduch, so as not to outshine another newly engaged chassan in town until that chassan's sheva brachos ended.

title.en: The spilled wine and the kashya in Nikolsburg

summary.en: Reb Akiva Eiger spills his own cup at the Seder so a poor guest who stained the tablecloth would not be ashamed, and in Nikolsburg he lets a kashya of Reb Mordechai Benet stand in public, revealing the answer only privately so the local Rav would not be lowered. The Rav concludes that great people had middos and derech eretz and would rather suffer than shame anyone.

title.en: Reb Yisrael Salanter on shaming and forgiveness

summary.en: Reb Yisrael Salanter leaves a yeshiva so a fellow maggid shiur would not be hurt, and after a wealthy man shames a former shoemaker at his daughter's wedding in Vilna, he says the rabbanim of the previous generation are being judged for not teaching good middos. The Rav then describes Reb Yisrael Salanter's disagreement with the Chafetz Chaim on whether one must ask forgiveness for lashon hara when it would only cause the victim pain.

title.en: A two-hour seudah for the maid's sake

summary.en: A wealthy host describes his five-hour Shabbos meal with glatt kosher meat, zemiros and divrei Torah; the Rav explains along the way what glatt kosher means and how it came to New York. Reb Yisrael Salanter agrees to come only if the meal lasts two hours, then asks the exhausted maid for forgiveness and shows the host that his extra zemiros came at her expense.

oneLiner.en: The Rav tells stories of Rebbes, among them a Rebbe who spent a night in a Vienna jail with a broken Jew and understood only years later, in America, why he had been there.

abstract.en: In this short recording the Rav tells a few stories, apparently about the Kapishnitzer Rebbe. He first describes a chuppah where several Rebbes were present and the Skverer Rebbe asked that the Satmar Rebbe, Reb Yoel, be called up for a brachah. He then tells, in a badly garbled stretch, of a father whose son was involved with a non-Jewish girl and who made an engagement party with much liquor, where the drunk guests began to insult Jews. The clearest story follows: the Rebbe was held one night in a jail in Vienna, and a Jew who had married out many years before was brought in and spent the night in anguish, crying out. The Rebbe was freed the next morning without understanding why he had to be there; only years later in America, when that Jew came to him with his son, did he understand.

en: At a chuppah where several Rebbes were present, the Skverer Rebbe asked that the Satmar Rebbe, Reb Yoel, be called up for a brachah.
A Rebbe spent one night in a Vienna jail, where a Jew who had married out many years before spent the night crying out in anguish.
Freed the next morning, the Rebbe did not understand why he had to be there; only in America, when the Jew came to him with his son, did he understand.

title.en: Stories of Rebbes and a night in jail

summary.en: The Rav describes a chuppah attended by several Rebbes, tells in garbled form of an engagement party where drunk guests insulted Jews, and then tells of a Rebbe's night in a Vienna jail with a Jew who had married out, whose purpose he understood only years later in America.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's emunah is a feeling of the heart inherited from the mother, so that even a Jewish apikorus believes deep down and only invents excuses, like the fox with his 'sour grapes'.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by contrasting a goy, who can grasp emunah through logic, with a Jew, who senses it by instinct. He illustrates instinct with the Chasam Sofer on a father who breaks into his son's home unaware: the son may not kill him, since the father's heart knows. Jews are Hashem's children and feel Him with the heart. The three matzos and four cups at the Seder stand for the Avos and the Imahos, mind and heart. A disciple feels his Rebbe, as the Lechovitcher felt the passing of Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin. Jewishness follows the mother because emunah, a feeling, comes from her, which the Rav also reads in the word emunah itself. Using Ben Sira's fable of the fox and the sour grapes, he shows how gaavah drives a person to justify himself: Esav blamed his wives, and the Jewish apikorus, who truly believes, denies only to follow his desires.

en: A goy can understand emunah through logic, but a Jew senses it by instinct, with his heart.
Just as a father's heart senses his son even when he does not know it is him, Jews, as Hashem's children, feel a bond with Him that goes beyond what the mind dictates.
The three matzos and four cups correspond to the Avos and Imahos: chochmah, the mind, and binah, the feeling of the heart, in which women are greater.
A child's Jewishness follows the mother because emunah is a feeling, and feeling comes from the mother.
Out of gaavah a person refuses to admit his own failure and blames something else, as the fox called the grapes sour.
A Jewish apikorus truly believes deep in his heart; he denies only because he wants to follow his desires.

title.en: A Jew's emunah is instinct

summary.en: The Rav contrasts a goy, who understands emunah through logic, with a Jew, who senses it by instinct. He brings the Chasam Sofer on a father who breaks into his son's home unaware that it is his son's: the son may not kill him, since the father's heart knows. The same feeling exists in animals, and Jews, as Hashem's children, feel Him with the heart.

title.en: Matzos and cups: mind and heart

summary.en: The Rav explains that the three matzos are the Avos and the four cups the Imahos, chochmah and binah. Facts of the mind are the same for everyone, while the heart leans by a person's nature, as with Beis Hillel. He brings that women were given extra binah, that grain gives understanding while wine stirs feeling, and ties this to the two shins of the tefillin and to the emunah in the heart inherited from Avraham.

title.en: The feeling of a wife and a disciple

summary.en: The Rav explains why one witness suffices to let a woman remarry: she feels whether her husband is alive. So too a disciple feels his bond to his Rebbe, and he tells how the Lechovitcher cried out that he no longer felt his Rebbe until he was told that Rabbi Shlomo of Karlin had passed away.

title.en: Why Jewishness follows the mother

summary.en: The Rav asks why a child's Jewishness is set by the mother when tribe and inheritance follow the father, and answers that emunah is a feeling, which comes from the mother. He then shows it in loshon hakodesh: when a verb ending in nun becomes a noun, the last nun falls away, as chanun becomes chen, shanun becomes shen and ganun becomes gan; so amun becomes em, mother.

title.en: Ben Sira's fable of the sour grapes

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's discussion of Ben Sira, who wrote fables of foxes that the nations later took over. He tells the fable of the fox who struggled for three days to climb a fence to reach grapes and then declared them sour, and explains that a person, out of gaavah, would rather blame the grapes than admit his own weakness.

title.en: Esav blames his wives

summary.en: The Rav relates that the Chazon Ish told a melamed who wanted to study psychology that everything can be learned from Chumash and Rashi. He then shows the same trait in the parsha: Esav saw that he lost the brachos and that Yaakov was sent to take a proper wife, concluded that his wives were to blame, and married the daughter of Yishmael, rather than admitting his own fault.

title.en: Rationalization and the Jewish apikorus

summary.en: The Rav gives examples of blaming others: the bachur who hits his finger and blames the hammer, the bachur who does not learn and blames the Rebbe and the classroom. This rationalization comes from gaavah, and it is why a Jewish apikorus, a child of the Avos, says he does not believe: he wants to follow his desires. He adds a joke about a man falling down the stairs and a philosopher's essay that there was never a true atheist.

title.en: The Six Day War and the letter about the beach

summary.en: The Rav recalls the danger before the Six Day War and the open miracles in it, such as a burning house whose fire was put out when a second bomb burst the water tank on the roof. He tells of a woman who wrote to a newspaper asking it to stop writing about the miracles, because they disturbed her driving to the beach on Shabbos; this, he concludes, is the Jewish apikorus, who believes but says 'sour grapes'.

catalogTitle: Ascribe Your Power and Accomplishments to Hashem (מזמור לדוד הבו פירושעל הפרק)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Mizmor l'Dovid Havu, the opening of Kabbalas Shabbos, as a call to ascribe every power, beauty and accomplishment in the world to Hashem, which is the meaning of resting from the 39 melachos on Shabbos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Mizmor l'Dovid Havu as the introduction to Kabbalas Shabbos: after six days of working and producing, a person must strengthen his emunah that everything comes from Hashem. 'Havu laShem bnei eilim' tells the powerful to ascribe their strength to Hashem. Going through the kapitel, he explains 'kol Hashem' as the Ten Utterances still hidden inside every force: the might of the ocean, of rulers, of beauty. One who sees Hashem in that power sweetens the din. The cedars that seem to block the heavens, like communist Russia, Yavan, Bavel and Rome, are broken by Hashem, so one should not panic before today's powers. Fire, the energy behind all four elements, is the same kol Hashem. Shabbos refutes man's claim to production: the 39 melachos, learned from the Mishkan, a miniature world, are the 39 curses after the sin, while Shabbos is blessing.

en: Mizmor l'Dovid Havu introduces Kabbalas Shabbos because after six days of production a person must strengthen his emunah that Hashem, not he, creates and provides everything.
'Havu laShem bnei eilim' calls on the powerful and respected to ascribe their strength and prowess to Hashem.
The 'kol Hashem' of the Ten Utterances is hidden in every force of nature and every human power, and a person must identify Hashem in it even where he cannot see Him.
Hashem breaks the 'cedars', the great powers that block the view of heaven, as history shows with Russia, Yavan, Bavel and Rome, so one should not panic before today's powers.
Shabbos is a refutation of man's claim that his own prowess and industry produced what he has.
The 39 melachos, learned from the Mishkan, are the activities Hashem put into the world and also the 39 curses given after the sin, while Shabbos is a day of blessing.

candidateTopics: Hashem hidden in the forces of nature
melachos as the curses of the sin

title.en: Havu laShem: ascribe your power to Hashem

summary.en: The Rav introduces Mizmor l'Dovid Havu as the preface to Kabbalas Shabbos: after six days of working a person must strengthen his emunah that everything comes from Hashem. He explains 'bnei eilim' as the powerful and respected, who must ascribe their strength to Hashem and bow before Him.

title.en: Kol Hashem in the waters and in every power

summary.en: The Rav explains 'kol Hashem al hamayim' as the Ten Utterances concealed in the force of the oceans and 'kol Hashem bakoach' as the power hidden in kings and rulers, citing the Nefesh HaChaim. He tells of a Rav who, fleeing the Nazis, kept in mind that their power was only Hashem's, and explains that recognizing this sweetens the din.

title.en: Beauty, cedars and looking up to heaven

summary.en: The Rav explains 'kol Hashem behadar' and 'shover arazim': the cedars symbolize mighty rulers like communist Russia, broken overnight. He explains why people look up to the sky for Hashem, brings the Gemara about davening in a room with windows, and shows how the cedars of a forest block the view of heaven, as Russia forbade belief.

title.en: Hashem breaks the cedars of Lebanon

summary.en: The Rav shows from history that Hashem breaks the cedars: Yavan, which made a god of beauty and might, and Bavel, Greece and Rome all vanished. He says one should not panic before today's powers, and explains 'vayarkidem kmo egel' as Hashem moving the boundaries of nations like a restless calf.

title.en: Flames of fire and Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains 'kol Hashem chotzev lahavos eish': fire is energy, the strongest of the four elements, and all energy in the world is the kol Hashem from the six days of creation. From here he explains Shabbos as a refutation of man's belief that his own prowess produces, and as the day of menuchah when one realizes Hashem did everything.

title.en: The 39 melachos learned from the Mishkan

summary.en: The Rav explains that on Shabbos one testifies that Hashem created the world by refraining from the 39 melachos with which He made it. Since no one witnessed creation, these are known from the Mishkan, a miniature world, whose work is detailed in the parshiyos of Terumah and Tetzaveh and defined in Maseches Shabbos, the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch.

title.en: The melachos are curses; Shabbos is blessing

summary.en: The Rav explains that the 39 melachos are 39 curses: before the sin bread and clothing grew on trees, and the Mishnah's melachos are the toil of producing bread and clothing that came with the curses. Shabbos is blessing, so it has no melachos; in the future, as the Gemara says, the land will again produce without work. He closes that one must bow to Hashem and proclaim that all power comes from Him.

oneLiner.en: Through a chain of stories about Chassidic and Lithuanian gedolim, the Rav shows how far tzaddikim went to guard another Jew's honor and never to shame him.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by recalling that this year's talks to the bachurim have dealt with kavod chaveirim, honoring one's fellow, a weak point in the generation before Moshiach, when the Gemara says chutzpah will increase. Instead of direct mussar he tells stories of tzaddikim, since tzaddikim said such stories strengthen emunah. He then tells a series of maasios: the Chiddushei HaRim refusing to count in a minyan a man who had slapped another Jew, and warning against calling someone by a nickname; the Divrei Chaim making his son-in-law pay for a whole wedding after shaming a poor man; Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan keeping a poor man's secret; the Dukla Rav eating a pot of kerosene-tainted cholent to protect a maid; the refinement of Kelm; Rabbi Shmuel Salant's answer to a simple woman and his rebuke of a proud baal tokea; how Rabbi Yisrael Salanter's concern for a wagon driver won over the future founder of Novardok; and the Chofetz Chaim expelling a chutzpadik bachur while keeping a thief, based on the Mishnah in Avos.

en: The Rav explains that in the time before Moshiach emunah is weak, and tzaddikim said that telling stories of tzaddikim strengthens it; therefore he tells stories rather than direct mussar.
Tzaddikim took extreme care not to come even into a doubt of shaming another Jew, as in the stories of Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan and the Divrei Chaim.
Working on mussar and kavod habriyos refines a person until he notices even fine points, like the smell of an extinguished havdalah candle bothering someone.
Rabbi Shmuel Salant taught that one may not embarrass anyone, especially someone who asks a foolish question, lest she be afraid to ask again.
Rabbi Yisrael Salanter interrupted an important mussar conversation so that a wagon driver would not be distressed, and seeing this made Rabbi Yosef Yoizel leave his business and become his talmid.
The Chofetz Chaim kept a bachur who stole but expelled one who spoke with chutzpah, because an az panim is presumed not to do teshuvah.

title.en: Honoring others and stories of tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav says this year's talks deal with kavod chaveirim, since chutzpah is a great test before Moshiach. He explains why he tells stories of tzaddikim instead of direct mussar: tzaddikim said such stories strengthen emunah, which will be very weak before Moshiach.

title.en: The Chiddushei HaRim's minyan and the nickname

summary.en: On his yahrzeit the Chiddushei HaRim wanted a small minyan; when a man forced his way in by slapping another Jew, the Rebbe refused to count him, citing Choshen Mishpat. He also warns a man who called a rav by a nickname, answering that Gehinom has room for everyone.

title.en: The Divrei Chaim and Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan

summary.en: The Divrei Chaim makes his son-in-law, who shamed a poor man collecting for his daughter's wedding, raise money for the whole wedding. Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan refuses to reveal the name of a ruined rich man even for a large donation, and the wealthy donor then reveals that he too is secretly poor.

title.en: The Dukla Rav's cholent and the refinement of Kelm

summary.en: Rabbi Avigdor Halberstam eats an entire pot of cholent tainted with kerosene so the host will not be angry at the maid. In Kelm, as Rabbi Yaakov Kamenetsky told, a forgotten yarmulke lay untouched for months, and the havdalah candle was put out outdoors so its smell would bother no one.

title.en: Rabbi Shmuel Salant: the cat and the shofar

summary.en: Rabbi Shmuel Salant answers a simple woman's foolish question about a cat with full seriousness so she will not be shamed. Then a young substitute baal tokea fails in the middle of the tekios, and Rabbi Shmuel tells him it was because he thought himself better than the old baal tokea.

title.en: Rabbi Yisrael Salanter and the Novardoker

summary.en: Rabbi Yosef Yoizel, a wealthy merchant, sees Rabbi Yisrael Salanter break off a mussar talk so a wagon driver would not be distressed, and leaves business to become his talmid and found the Novardok yeshivos. Later Rabbi Yoizel rebukes a man who shamed another and claimed it was worth losing Olam Haba.

title.en: Rabbi Elya Lopian and the Chofetz Chaim's ruling

summary.en: Rabbi Elya Lopian's wife is healed by a stranger he understood to be Eliyahu HaNavi, and the Sfas Emes knew of it. Rabbi Elya then relates, from the Chofetz Chaim's son-in-law, that the Chofetz Chaim kept a thief in yeshiva but expelled a bachur who spoke with chutzpah, explaining it from the Mishnah 'az panim l'Gehinom'.

oneLiner.en: Speaking at the resting place of Shimon HaTzaddik as a new zman of learning begins, the Rav explains how place, time and soul come together in a time of Divine favor, and calls for early prayer and strengthened yiras Shamayim in a dangerous time.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a l'chaim and a prayer at the resting place of Shimon HaTzaddik. Using the threefold division of olam, shanah and nefesh (place, time and soul), he notes that parshas Re'eh introduces 'the place Hashem will choose', while the coming forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul are a time of favor that Moshe Rabbeinu's prayer established. Shimon HaTzaddik is the 'soul' of favor: Rav Yehoshua Leib Diskin sent people to pray there, and in time of war a Rebbe sent people there rather than only to the Kosel. He began the toil and chiddushim of the Oral Torah and is the first named in Pirkei Avos, so it is a fitting place to pray for success at the start of a new zman. The Rav then ties this week's middah of tiferes to Torah through the haftarah, counts the mentions of 'the chosen place' and of simchah in the parsha, and turns to the dangers facing Jews, urging prayer before trouble and strength against today's trials, citing the Akeidah. He closes with the hillula of the Satmar Rav and a story of his ruach hakodesh.

en: Every matter exists in place, time and soul; parshas Re'eh reveals a 'place of favor', Elul is a 'time of favor', and Shimon HaTzaddik is the 'soul' through which favor comes.
The novelty of Moshe Rabbeinu's last forty days is that after the sin of the Golden Calf a time of favor came into being, from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, established through his prayer.
The toil, pilpul and chiddushim of the Oral Torah began with Shimon HaTzaddik, which is why tzaddikim called his resting place the cradle of the Oral Torah.
One must pray before trouble arrives, because once harsh judgment rules it is harder for prayer to be accepted.
Hashem placed this generation among great trials in tznius, guarding the eyes and guarding thought, and withstanding them through yiras Shamayim is its task.
